#2595. Is Hamilton and Leclerc's Ferrari partnership sustainable? F1 Q&A

Max Verstappen triumphed in a thrilling Las Vegas Grand Prix ahead of the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

There were 34 lead changes across the 50 laps of racing as Dutchman Verstappen held off attacks from Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, plus his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar.

Ferrari had to deal with another intra-team battle on track as Charles Leclerc received a 10-second time penalty after colliding with Lewis Hamilton.

Here, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

Verstappen a constant amid chaos as he says Russell is 'so far below my level'

After Las Vegas, have Ferrari now reached a crossroads? With Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc's on-track antics, is their partnership sustainable? Should Ferrari consider a change of direction, potentially bringing Oliver Bearman into the equation? - Michael

The battle between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc at Ferrari is one that keeps on giving - but not in a way Ferrari would want.

The collision in Las Vegas for which Leclerc was penalised was just the latest flashpoint for the team in a season that has been full of them.

The drivers argued over race strategy in relation to each other in Zandvoort and Singapore.

Hamilton made an aggressive dive down the inside at the first chicane on the first lap at Monza, only for Leclerc to shove him on to the gravel.

Hamilton ignored calls to pit in both Singapore (because he didn't want to just circulate behind Leclerc) and Brazil (because, he said, he had not been given enough information about the weather).

There was the first-lap incident at Turn Four in Mexico in which their fighting led to both going off track and letting in Max Verstappen to win a race Ferrari should have finished one-two.

And now Las Vegas, where first Hamilton earned a 10-second penalty for gaining a position on Lando Norris on track in an incident that also involved Leclerc, then Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for tipping Hamilton into a spin later in the race.

Leclerc was on the receiving end of team principal Frederic Vasseur's ire in Las Vegas - the Frenchman calling the situation "unacceptable". But inside Ferrari they felt both drivers had a degree of culpability for the Mexico situation.

Somehow Vasseur needs to get a handle on this.

Ferrari want to allow them to race. And it's hard to imagine two drivers of such standing would accept anything else.

The problem is that doing so, amid their battle for supremacy within the team, is harming the team's results.

The concern for Ferrari is this is happening when there is relatively little at stake. It's easy to imagine how combustible it could become if Ferrari have a car capable of challenging for the title next year.

Both want to be the driver to deliver that next championship, for very different reasons.

Hamilton would get his eighth, which he feels he was unfairly denied in Abu Dhabi in 2021. And Leclerc would win his first, and complete the journey of being the first Ferrari academy driver to win the world championship for the team.

At the moment, this is not an existential question, but it's easy to see how it could become one, and Ferrari left with a decision of it being one or the other if they can't find a way to race without compromising the team.

Both drivers have buy into that and, as Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have largely done at McLaren, accept there will be days when they have to sacrifice themselves for the greater good of Ferrari while ensuring they are ahead of the other more often than not on speed and fair racing.

It's then up to the team to decide when there comes a point to impose team orders if either or both are in a title fight with another driver.

It remains to be seen whether either of them can fully buy into that in circumstances when they individually end up losing out.

Why does George Russell often feel the need to try mind games and make comments, such as those about Max Verstappen? It often backfires on him and are usually made when he's got nothing to race for. Shouldn't he focus on himself? - Nick

This, as Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff pointed out after the race in Las Vegas, is a rivalry that goes back years.

"They've known each other so long," was Wolff's verdict. "Since karting. I think it's probably been a bit of cat and mouse. Provocations on either side. Another good factor of entertainment."

Verstappen also had a bit of a set-to with Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson in Mexico practice, which was not dissimilar in some ways.

There, stewards ruled that both had driven in an "unacceptable manner" and both drivers admitted their moves had been unnecessary and clumsy.

There's no question Russell believed what he was saying about Verstappen's driving in final practice at Las Vegas. According to the stewards, he was in the right, as Verstappen was given a warning for his changing direction in the braking zone.

Are these mind games? Or just Russell saying what he thinks? He feels he has a valid point to make.

Making it in public does not seem to affect Verstappen in any way. Does it change anything? Verstappen is a remorseless, ruthless competitor on track whether he is provoked or not.

Yes, he admitted satisfaction when he saw Russell make his late-race error in Las Vegas. But did he race any differently because of the Briton's comments? That's unlikely. Verstappen was just doing what he felt was right to win the race.

Ultimately, it's Russell's career, and it's up to him how he conducts himself, what he chooses to say in public and what he does not.

Track design, cold temperatures, energy deployment strategies or just the unwillingness of one team-mate to hold station behind another. What was the dominant factor in Las Vegas that led to such a hectic race? - Tim

The extraordinary Las Vegas race, with long trains of cars unable to break free of each other, was a combination of technical factors. Nothing to do with the willingness or otherwise of team-mates to hold station.

It was a combination of the track characteristics, particularly the long straights, the energy deployment demands of the engines, which are energy starved, and the cold temperatures and track surface and the effect they had on tyre behaviour.

As Max Verstappen said: "It was just the tow (in) combination with the deployment. Of course, when you are within a second, you have the overtake mode as well, and around here that is powerful. So, you could not pull away."

The tow provided a significant lap time gain of well over 0.5secs a lap. That's why a car in front could not pull away from a car behind even if it was slightly quicker.

The overtake mode provides an extra 0.5MJ of electrical energy per lap for a car following another by under a second. So that's another factor preventing someone pulling away.

Then the batteries were running out before the end of the straights, so a car running in front in free air was suffering from that, too.

On top of that, Las Vegas is a smooth track which is light on tyres. So degradation was almost non-existent. That kept tyre temperatures under control and allowed people to push hard throughout.

If the tyres had shown their usual behaviour of surface overheating leading to sliding, there would have been less action as drivers would have found it much harder to follow each other closely. As is usually the case in F1.

Drivers have been pushing for years for tyres to behave in this way, but so far Pirelli has been unable or unwilling to provide them. It only happens occasionally in specific circumstances.

The flip side of the argument is that so-called zero-deg races are sometimes boring as much as they are sometimes great, because drivers pushing to the limit can means less overtaking. Not in this case, though

Verstappen's superb racecraft & Russell's costly mistake - driver ratings

With a move to engines with a smaller electrical component in 2030, are F1 cars becoming less relevant to modern road cars? The argument was always that F1 is the test bed for future road car technology. - Paul

The current F1 engines, with a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, were decided upon five or so years ago when the road-car market was slightly different to now.

The push for electrification is still there, and will continue. But consumer take-up of electric cars, especially in the performance market, has not been what manufacturers expected. Hence a slight shift in focus.

That said, it's not as if the current F1 engines are especially road relevant. With a few exceptions, road cars tend to be either full electric, plug-in hybrid, where the electrical element is much less than 50-50, or full internal combustion.

So there is an argument the new engines, with sustainable fuel and a hybrid element that is about 12-13% of total output normally or 25% when on overtake mode, are more relevant to road cars, not less, at least in their fundamental architecture.

If this can get to a point where it is available to the mass market - and F1 is simplifying the demands on its make-up for the next ruleset in an attempt to help make the fuel more cost-effective for exactly that reason - it could be a game-changer for emissions in the road-car market.

That's because there will inevitably be a lot of legacy internal combustion vehicles on the road globally for many years, even after the new-car market becomes fully electric.

So if emissions from these can be reduced by 80%, as is the ballpark figure for the carbon-impact reduction of sustainable fuels versus fossil fuels, that's a major step.

Don't forget, too, the 2030 rules were the product of talks between the manufacturers and the FIA.

It was the manufacturers who pushed back against FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem's initial desire for a naturally aspirated engine with no hybrid element.

And they did that exactly because it made them more road relevant.

#2593. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2589. PSV manager Peter Bosz explains what he admires most about Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho: ‘He has a very recognisable style’

PSV Eindhoven manager Peter Bosz has expressed his admiration for Jose Mourinho ahead of Tuesday's Champions League meeting with Real Madrid, describing the Portuguese coach's achievements as incredible while acknowledging their contrasting football philosophies.

Speaking at the pre-match press conference, Bosz praised Mourinho's ability to evolve throughout his managerial career and admitted that he has previously studied his methods to improve his own coaching.

The Dutch manager also recognised the challenge awaiting his team against a Real Madrid side chasing a tenth consecutive victory across all competitions.

Bosz was particularly impressed by Mourinho's longevity and ability to remain successful despite changes in football.

The PSV manager believes continuous development and adapting to different circumstances are essential qualities behind the Portuguese coach's achievements.

"Mourinho also has a very recognisable style; he prepares his players very well, and we know what to expect. I don't think anyone can be as successful as he is without constantly developing; I do the same myself.

"I try to learn, but he has certain benchmarks; it's incredible what he has achieved in his professional career, and you can't achieve that unless you adapt to new situations," he explained.

Peter Bosz has nothing but praise for Real Madrid manager Jose Mourinho. (Photo by Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty Images)

The PSV coach also revealed that Mourinho's approach has influenced his own thinking, although he does not necessarily share the Real Madrid manager's methods.

"I want to learn from him; you learn from his lessons. I used to study what he said, and that's the message I want to convey to my players.

"He's a very interesting manager. I have no negative comments about him; we have different personalities. He has to do whatever it takes to win; I have a different philosophy.

"I'm not saying he does it wrong, but I work differently. We're very different people, but I have great respect for him," he noted.

Bosz also acknowledged the consistency of Mourinho's team, particularly their ability to find victories even when matches become difficult.

Real Madrid's determination to keep fighting until the final whistle is something the Dutchman believes deserves recognition.

"I think they're playing well; they've had nine wins, some of them in the dying minutes, which is positive because it shows they keep fighting until the very end to win.

Real Madrid will host PSG later today. (Photo by Angel Martinez/Getty Images)

"We've been playing in the Champions League for four years now; we've played in big stadiums – this one is spectacular, but we've been in others before."

The PSV manager also dismissed the idea that his players needed additional motivation to face Real Madrid's biggest stars, particularly Kylian Mbappe.

"Everyone knows Kylian Mbappe and I don't think I need to say much to motivate them; they know the Real Madrid players and know exactly what to do tomorrow," he explained.

Although Bosz wants his team to maintain its attacking identity, he acknowledged that facing Real Madrid requires a degree of tactical flexibility.

The Dutchman explained that adapting to opponents has always been part of his preparation rather than something reserved for particularly difficult fixtures.

"I always say this: I adapt to the opposition all the time; we did so last weekend, but we have our own footballing philosophy and I want to stick to it.

"However, we have to adapt, especially against Real Madrid, because they are a very strong side with players of great quality," he concluded.

#2587. Making sense of Liam Coen's nonsensical decision to kick a late field goal

Jacksonville’s loss to the Giants on Sunday included a nonsensical decision with 3:43 to play. Down by eight points and facing fourth and goal from the New York eight, Jaguars coach Liam Coen decided to kick a field goal.

After the game, Jaguars coach Liam Coen justified the decision to take the three points by calling an effort to score a touchdown a “hope play.”

We hope he’s not serious. It was eight yards, not 80. Regardless of what the analytics said, it was time to go for the touchdown, which with a successful two-point conversion would have tied the game.

As explained on Monday’s PFT Live, I think the two-point conversion was the deciding factor for Coen. When the score was 23-9, the Jaguars scored a touchdown that cut the margin to eight. After the touchdown, Coen played the all-too-common analytics game, opting to go for two in the hopes of cutting the margin to six and ideally avoiding overtime if they had scored again.

When it was time to go for two, Coen utilized his best two-point play based on the specific matchup of the Jacksonville offense against the New York defense. It failed. Which meant that, if/when the Jaguars scored another touchdown, they would need to rely on Coen’s second-best two-point play.

After Plan A failed, why would Coen believe Plan B would succeed?

And so instead of going for a touchdown which may or may not have been capped by a successful two-point try, Coen opted to take the three and kick off. Which pissed off the New York offense, and which helped set the stage for the Jaguars never getting the ball again.

If the Jaguars had gone for the score, the Giants would have gotten the ball deep in their own end. The Jaguars would have been likely to get another shot at a touchdown and a two-point conversion.

Still, the Jaguars would have had to convert a two-point play after their best option at going for two had failed. In the moment, that reality may have been the difference for Coen.

Which brings us back to the analytics-driven trend to go for two after scoring a touchdown when trailing by 14. If the two-pointer fails, the coach needs to be confident in the second-best two-point play for the week. Coen likely wasn’t, which contributed to the decision to not try to gain eight yards in a one-score game.

That’s the most important factor when it comes to relying on math. Once teams start down the go-for-two path, their confidence (or lack thereof) in the potential for successful two-point plays becomes critical.

Coen’s best two-point play failed. Which may have shaken his faith in his second-best two-point play. Which may have prompted him to opt for the three points in lieu of rolling the dice on scoring from the eight — before rolling the dice on scoring again from the two.

#2579. Monday Night Football: Bengals lead 10-7 at halftime

It took more than a quarter and a half for any points to get scored in Washington on Monday night, but the Bengals and Commanders finally got going in the final minutes before halftime.

After a 15-play drive resulted in a field goal midway through the second quarter, the Bengals found more explosive plays on their next possession. Running back Samaje Perine broke free on a short pass for a 44-yard gain and Joe Burrow then went deep to wide receiver Tee Higgins for a 31-yard touchdown on the first play after the two-minute warning. The catch bore some resemblance to the one by Jaguars wideout Parker Washington that was ruled incomplete on Sunday, but there was no review.

That score put the Bengals up 10-0 and left the Commanders with a last chance to find their first points of the evening.

Jayden Daniels ran for one first down and threw for two more before hooking up with tight end Chig Okonkwo for a 32-yard gain that moved the Commanders to Cincinnati’s 6-yard-line. A pass to wide receiver Treylon Burks in the end zone drew a pass interference flag on cornerback Dax Hill and running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt punched the ball in on the next play to make it 10-7 going into the break.

Daniels is 8-of-11 for 85 yards, but has been sacked three times by Boye Mafe. The last of those came on a third down and led to an animated Stefon Diggs appearing to yell about throwing the ball on the sideline while the Bengals had possession. Diggs’s only catch of the half came on the late touchdown drive.

Burrow is 16-of-23 for 179 yards and has been sacked a couple of times. The Bengals also saw safety Bryan Cook leave just before halftime with an ankle injury and he’s called questionable to be back on the field when the Commanders get the ball to start the second half.

#2578. Josh Kushner and Bob Iger spotted at Lakers-Jazz game

Josh Kushner and Bob Iger attended the Los Angeles Lakers vs. Utah Jazz game alongside Lakers governor Jeanie Buss on Monday, Nov. 23. The trio was seen sitting among the crowd at Crypto.com Arena.

It was the first game they've attended since agreeing in August to purchase the team from Mark Walter at a $12.5 billion valuation. Kushner and Iger have talked with Buss about her role with the organization throughout the sale process.

Kushner also went through the franchise's "back-of-house space" with Rob Pelinka, the Lakers president of basketball operations and general manager, according to ESPN's Dave McMenamin.

Jerry West (#44) played 14 seasons from 1960-1974 with the Lakers and was a force who never left the NBA once he got there, according to USA Today's Jeff Zillgitt. The Hall of Famer, pictured here in action against the Cincinnati Royals, was remembered for his imprint as a shooting guard and builder of teams. His impact remains visible in today’s NBA and he went on to touch generations of teams and players, including LeBron James, who talked to West about winning and losing.

The Lakers often believed that Elgin Baylor (#22) remained under appreciated during his 14-year NBA career with the franchise in Minneapolis and Los Angeles. Baylor, pictured Feb. 17, 1970, in a game against the New York Knicks, is among six Lakers luminaries to have a statue outside of Staples Center, and is also among 10 Lakers players to have their jersey retired. Baylor entered the Naismith Memorial Hall of Fame after winning an NBA championship (1972), posted an NBA Finals record 61 points in Game 5 of the 1961 NBA Finals against Boston, winning the league’s rookie of the year award (1959) and making 11 All-Star appearances.

Los Angeles Lakers center #13 Wilt Chamberlain scored 31,419 points, averaging 30.1 ppg, during 1,045 games over a 16-year Hall of Fame career. Chamberlain led the NBA in scoring seven straight years, averaged 50.4 points per game in 1962 and scored a record 100 points in a single game on March 2, 1962 against the New York Knicks in Hershey, Pennsylvania. The NBA didn’t televise the game and less than 5,000 people got to witness the iconic moment. HoopsHype ranked the top 80 players in NBA history and Chamberlain came in ranked No. 6 on the list, according to Sixers Wire.

Los Angeles Lakers center #33 Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, pictured in action during the 1981-82 season in Indianapolis, is one of the greatest basketball players in history – from his days as a prep star in New York City at Power Memorial Academy to his three NCAA championships and 88-2 record at UCLA and his six NBA championships and six MVPs with the Milwaukee Bucks and Los Angeles Lakers. He averaged at least 21 points in his first 17 seasons, averaged at least 12 rebounds in his first 10 seasons and shot at least 50% from the field.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Magic Johnson (32) in action against the Detroit Pistons during the 1988 NBA Finals at the Silverdome. Magic was the face of the Lakers and the NBA during much of the 1980s when he won five NBA titles and led the "Showtime" teams in legendary showdowns with Larry Bird and the Celtics. The Hall of Famer was a three-time NBA MVP and is regarded as one of the best point guards ever to play the game.

Los Angeles Lakers' Kobe Bryant soars to the basket against Sacramento Kings's Mike Bibby during Game 4 of the NBA Western Conference finals in Los Angeles, May 26, 2002. Kobe spent all 20 years of his legendary career with the Lakers, won five championships, and is the fourth-leading scorer in NBA history. One of the fiercest competitors to play the game, Kobe could do it all. His legend in Lakers Nation will live on forever.

Los Angeles Lakers forward James Worthy celebrates his team's series-clinching victory over the Portland Trail Blazers in Game 6 of the NBA Western Conference Finals at the Great Western Forum in Inglewood, Calif. on May 30, 1991. James Worthy was a cornerstone of the Los Angeles Lakers’ “Showtime” era, helping the franchise win three NBA championships in the 1980s. Known for his clutch performances and smooth all-around game, the Hall of Famer remains one of the most celebrated players in Lakers history.

#2577. Lighting error briefly leaves Commanders-Bengals ‘MNF’ game in dark as Roger Goodell looks on

Billy Joel once sang about seeing the lights go down on Broadway, and now football fans can say they saw the lights go down at Northwest Stadium.

The "Monday Night Football" game between the Bengals and Commanders was briefly delayed after the lights went out in the middle of the third quarter just as Jayden Daniels was lining up to hike the ball on third-and-14.

Stadium lights turn off during the third quarter between the Cincinnati Bengals and Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The ESPN broadcast initially reported that the issue was "power-related and not the stadium" and later added that it had occurred due to "regularly scheduled maintenance for 10 p.m." by the "lighting vendor" that was never disabled.

"It's a weekday thing, and they forgot it was a Monday night game," ESPN broadcaster Joe Buck said on the broadcast.

All the lights in the stadium went out at first, causing the refs to blow the whistle with 11:59 left in the third quarter. After several seconds, the electric signage that wraps around the stadium and the video board came back on, providing some light inside the Landover, Maryland venue.

"Somebody turned out the lights," Buck said.

The telecast showed Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow throwing a football around to keep warm.

NFL commissioner Roger Goodell was also on hand in the suit of Commanders owner Josh Harris.

ESPN threw to commercials after several moments and when the network returned, the lights also returned.

The Bengals were holding a 10-7 lead at the time of the power outage and when play resumed, Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels was forced to throw the ball away. The Commanders rallied to win the game 22-20 on a walk-off field goal that came with some clock controversey.

The Cincinnati Bengals and the Washington Commanders stand on the field after the lights went off during a game in Landover, Md., Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. Getty Images

NFL commissioner Roger Goodell looks on as the lights go out during Commanders-Bengals. ESPN/X

Washington settled for a field goal that briefly tied the game at 10-10.

Monday's incident is just the latest to occur at the outdated home of the Commanders.

On Jan. 2, 2022, a railing broke at what was then known as FedEx Field sending several football fans tumbling in a near-tragic incident.

Players look on after the lights go out during the third quarter of the game between the Cincinnati Bengals and Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Raw sewage soaked fans in one section of the stadium during a game against the Chargers after a pipe burst on Sept. 12, 2021.

The Commanders are building a new stadium at the site of the former RFK Stadium in Washington, D.C., that is scheduled to open in 2030.

Speaking with ESPN ahead of the game, Goodell expressed excitement over the new stadium.

"I'm a kid who grew up here. And so I remember going to RFK Stadium. And I think the work that they've done just on the architectural side of it and the construction of it, I think it's going to be remarkable," the NFL commissioner said, according to Front Office Sports.." And having it on the same site, I think it's going to have a wonderful emotional connection. Being in the District is special. And I just think that's going to be a wonderful moment, not only for the league but for the fans."

#2576. What Tommy Lloyd and JJ Mandaquit said after Arizona’s Maui Invitational win over Colorado State

As expected, Arizona had a very large contingent of fans in attendance inside the tiny Lahaina Civic Center on Monday night. That included roughly 50 that were there to see JJ Mandaquit, a Hawai'i native playing for the first time in his home state.

All those dressed in red were treated to a 96-83 win over Colorado State in the nightcap of the Maui Invitational's first day. It was the 16th win in 20 tries for Tommy Lloyd in the tournament, including a 4-0 record with the Wildcats.

The UA played the late game Monday but will be in the second semifinal on Tuesday, set for 3 p.m. MT against Providence.

Our game recap can be found here, and below is what Lloyd and Mandaquit said afterwards:

Lloyd on the win: "Obviously we got the result we we wanted to get. I want to give a ton of credit to Colorado State. I mean they came out and they really hung with it. We got a good lead on them, and that go one or two ways, and they responded."

On Colorado State's offense: "I'll just say this: I've done this a long time, and they run their stuff as well as anybody. They can really direct the ball and find shots where they want to find them and they just do a good job getting deep into their actions and and having kind of layers to what they do. It was impressive to play against, I give our guys credit because it's not easy to guard, for hanging in there."

On defending the 3-point shot: "We wish we played better defense in the second half. But in these tournaments, and in Maui, I don't know if you always win with your defense in Maui. So you got to keep scoring points. We were able to do that, and we're excited to play a good Providence team tomorrow."

On Mandaquit scoring a career-high 15: "JJ's played on the big stage, in USA Basketball, obviously competing for state championships, and playing elite high school basketball. So I wasn't concerned with him being distracted here, being nervous. I mean, he's a hooper, and you can really see and feel his confidence growing on a daily basis."

On not using the bench as much as hoped: "I don't set like kind of a preset menu, so to speak. I mean, it's how the game goes. I don't assume because you have a 16-point lead in halftime, you're gonna have a 32-point lead at the end of the game. It's just not how it goes, and there's always a chance a team makes a run at you, and Colorado State did. I mean, we got it up to 23 early in the second half. You'd like to put the pedal to the metal a little bit there, but I think they came on a run like they scored seven or nine points in a row to kind of respond, I think it was a 9-0 run. So then they got back in the game. I think at one time they cut it to seven. But, I tell our guys all the time that's why you build a lead. You build a lead to be able to kind of withstand some runs and put yourself in position to win the game down the stretch. And, I thought our guys did a good job kind of controlling the game down the stretch."

On making adjustments between games: "These deals move fast. I mean, we play in like 14 hours or something. I don't even know what time it is. Tomorrow we're just going to tee it up. I mean, we honestly haven't done anything to prepare for Providence up to this point. I'm sure our guys have done some advanced scouting on them and watched them a little bit. But we'll meet with the team tonight. Probably start talking a little bit about what a plan could be. We'll kind of firm it up in the morning, and then we'll tip the ball up. So you don't have a lot of time to make like tactical changes, or anything like that. But that being said, we've practiced and and we're prepared for these quick turnarounds. I can't wait till noon tomorrow."

On playing a late game: "We're used to playing late. Fortunately in Arizona, we get on national TV a lot, and when you're on national TV a lot, you don't have a lot of say in your game times. So we're used to playing 8 o'clock, 9 o'clock, whenever, and when we play early, whatever the game time is, we'll do the best to be ready to play."

On Motiejus Krivas' performance: "Mo had some jaw-dropping moments. But I don't know if you can make two threes and miss three free throws. I don't know if that's allowed. Mo's a really good player, and Mo can shoot threes, but Mo doesn't play the game for himself. He plays the game for the team, and we have other guys that they're probably maybe a little bit better 3-point shooters than him, and they can't do what he does inside. He's so unique in what he can do, you know, and the attention that he draws, that you know he creates so much value for us down around the basket. I think that will always be his bread and butter."

On Krivas' one-handed dunk in transition: "I've had the good fortune of watching him play a lot of basketball for four years. He can really dunk hard with his left hand off his right foot. I mean, he probably does it better going left than he would right. So the stars finally aligned for him to show the world. I know that it kind of woke our Arizona crowd up a little bit. We have a great contingent here. Might have had a few too many mai tais early in the day. Felt a little sleepy, a little too much beach time. So hopefully the noon tip off … in Arizona, we go to bed early, there's no doubt about that. But I thought they were a little sleepy tonight. Then Mo woke them up a little bit. But I got faith our fans will be ready to rock tomorrow."

Mandaquit on playing at home: "It's amazing, it's an awesome experience. This is something I dreamed about as a little kid, and so to be back home playing at the college level on national television, it's everything I could have dreamed of."

On not being distracted: "Just keeping the main thing the main thing. We're here to play basketball, to win the tournament, and that's what comes first. Just keep my focus on the team, on our game plan, and making sure we execute."

On getting to play on the big stage: "Just keep believing, but you got to put in the work to match your dreams. It's not going to be easy, but if you keep showing up every day, sacrificing and putting in the work, good things will happen."

On playing in a tourney he watched on TV growing up: "It's a different feeling. It's my first college game back at home, and just trying to soak it all in, have fun. But like I said, keep the keep the main thing the main thing, and just try to execute the game plan. But definitely have fun doing it."

#2575. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2574. Tee Higgins touchdown highlights inconsistency of replay review

Just when we thought we were out when it comes to not knowing what a catch is, they pull us back in.

The past two days have included three examples of plays that make more confusing the question of whether a player has completed the act of catching the ball — and whether replay review was properly used to correct rulings made on the field.

It started on Sunday afternoon, when an apparent touchdown catch by Jaguars receiver Parker Washington was ruled not a catch on the field, with replay review not overturning the ruling. Even though the visual evidence seemed to provide clear and obvious proof that the ball was caught.

On Sunday night, 49ers receiver Mike Evans bobbled his way to a touchdown catch. He quite possibly didn’t get two feet in bounds after finally securing control of the ball. The play wasn’t even reviewed.

On Monday night, Bengals receiver Tee Higgins made a touchdown catch even though the ball was moving as he landed on the ground and out of bounds. There was no replay review.

The common denominator in these plays (beyond the fact that they involved potential touchdown catches) is the shadowy, uncertain replay process. As one head coach explained it to PFT on Monday (before the Bengals-Commanders game), it’s still not known who is making the decisions in New York as to what will be reviewed and what the outcome of the review will be.

It’s another reason for the NFL to embrace full transparency when it comes to replay review. We need to know who is making the decisions. We need to know their names. We need to hear their voices.

And we also need to know why — as happened in the case of the Evans and Higgins touchdowns — there was no full-blown review.

#2573. Commanders QB Jayden Daniels hits a pair of big passes to set up game-winning field goal to beat Bengals

It looked like Joe Burrow might have added to his MVP résumé by leading a game-winning drive. But Jayden Daniels got the last word.

After the Cincinnati Bengals kicked a field goal with 46 seconds left to take a 20-19 lead, Daniels hit two huge passes downfield to get the Washington Commanders in range for a short field goal and the win. Drew Stevens made the kick and Washington escaped with a 22-20 win.

The Bengals had a shot to end the game but couldn't run more time off the clock after getting in field-goal range. That allowed Daniels a shot. He hit rookie Antonio Williams for 22 yards and then 42 yards to set up the win on Stevens' 26-yard field goal.

Burrow had taken over as the MVP favorite before Monday night's game. But Daniels has had moments as a special quarterback, too, and he and Williams had a magical couple of plays to pull out a dramatic win.

The game didn't start with the Bengals tearing up a defense, as has been the case in recent weeks. The game was scoreless after the first quarter, mostly due to rain. That affected both offenses, though the weather cleared up and both teams started to move the ball better.

The Bengals took a 10-0 lead on a great catch in the end zone by Tee Higgins for a 31-yard score.

The Commanders had their protection issues in the first half, most notably blocking Boye Mafe who had three sacks before halftime. But a long drive near the end of the first half resulted in a Jacory Croskey-Merritt touchdown, and early in the first half a 47-yard run by Daniels set up a game-tying field goal.

The Bengals had been one of the hottest offenses in the NFL but the Commanders did a good job keeping pressure on Burrow and containing him, with an assist from the weather early in the game.

The Bengals got a touchdown to take the lead in the third quarter, as Burrow hit rookie Colbie Young for a 4-yard score after the QB was chased out of the pocket. But the Bengals couldn't do much else for most of the second half.

Part of the problem is they can't run the ball, and have given up trying. The Commanders had a good plan against a pass-heavy offense and the Bengals didn't have a counter-punch. That could end up being a problem for Cincinnati in the playoffs.

The Commanders weren't doing much themselves on offense, but had a couple field goals to keep them in the game. Then came a long drive at the right time. Highlighted by Stefon Diggs' 29-yard catch on second-and-20, the Commanders chewed up a lot of clock and took a lead. The Commanders had a big decision, whether to go for it on fourth-and-1 with less than two minutes left. Washington kicked the field goal for the 19-17 lead, but that left Burrow 2:26 to get in field-goal range and retake the lead.

Burrow got the drive going with a 12-yard pass to Higgins, and then he hit tight end Mike Gesicki for 32 yards. That put the Bengals in field-goal range and led to the Commanders starting to call their timeouts. There was almost a game-ending mistake from Burrow, but rookie linebacker Sonny Styles had a pass go off his hands and it was incomplete rather than an interception. Then Burrow took a sack, which was a loss of eight yards and made the field goal harder. McPherson came on for a 56-yard attempt and he nailed it. At that point it seemed like Cincinnati would escape.

Daniels had 46 seconds to answer. And he did, going to the middle of the field twice for Williams for big gains. Williams told ESPN afterward that the Commanders ran the same play for both catches.

The win helped the Commanders improve to 4-5-1. Washington still has a ways to go to get back in the NFC East race, but Daniels will do his best to keep the Commanders in it.

Antonio Williams finished the night with 9 catches for 122 yards, including 64 on Washington's game-winning drive.

Drew Stevens connected on all five of his field-goal attempts, including a walk-off winner.

And Jayden Daniels delivered when it mattered most. He finished the night completing 23 of 35 passes for 289 yards while adding 55 yards on the ground, including a 47-yard run that set up a Washington score.

What way to cap Week 11 with one of the unlikeliest wins of the season.

Jayden Daniels found Antonio Williams for a 22-yard gain and then a 44-yard gain to get the Commanders in field goal territory despite starting the possession with no timeouts and 46 seconds left on the clock.

Drew Stevens delivered with a walk-off field goal from 26 yards out to cap a stunning, 22-20 come-from-behind Commanders win.

Joe Burrow took a sack to push a field-goal attempt back to 56 yards, but Evan McPherson delivered.

The Bengals kicker was pure from long distance, and the Bengals are back on top with a 20-19 lead. Washington has 46 seconds to answer.

The Bengals have moved the ball into field-goal range, and the Commanders just missed a golden opportunity at an interception. The ball bounced off of Sonny Style's fingertips then through the hands of Rasul Douglas, who had a play on the ball.

Washington had a decision with fourth-and-less-than-yard in field-goal territory.

Dan Quinn decided to take the points after Stefon Diggs came up just short of a first down from the Cincinnati 24-yard line, and Drew Stevens delivered with a 41-yard field goal.

The score gives the commanders a 19-17 lead, but Joe Burrow and the Bengals have the ball and 2:26 remaining on the clock in need of just a field goal to re-take the lead. A first down would have given the Commanders a chance to burn clock and score a touchdown.

Stefon Diggs, who's been animated with his frustration all night, just got the Commanders over midfield on a big pass play with a chance to take a fourth-quarter lead.

The Commanders should keep throwing it to Chig Okonkwo.

Cincinnati's offense is suddenly toothless again. The Bengals punted after five plays, and the Commanders have the ball back with 8:30 remaining and a 17-16 deficit.

If they Commanders lose, they're gonna look back on some missed opportunities.

Jayden Daniels scrambled to buy time on third-and-goal, but his pass to Stefon Diggs in the end zone bounced short off the turf.

Drew Stevens instead connected from 25 yards to cap a third consecutive Washington possesion with a field goal, and Cincinnati remains in front, 17-16.

"The official word is the lighting vendor never disabled the regularly scheduled maintenance for 10 p.m. It's a weekday thing, and they forgot that it was a Monday night game."

Chase beat double coverage and had a chance for a big gain, but the ball was just out of his grasp. The result is a 3-and-out punt for the Bengals and a chance for Washington to take the lead with a 17-13 deficit.

OK, that didn't take long. The stadium lights were back in playing condition in just a few minutes.

#2571. Lakers honor Lawrence Tanter with video tribute, commemorative banner

The Lakers honored Lawrence Tanter with a video tribute on Monday as the Lakers played the Jazz.

The video included footage of Tanter introducing Magic Johnson, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Shaquille O'Neal, Kobe Bryant, LeBron James and Luka Doncic, as well as his signature "Laker girl" call and a banner drop over his 43 years as the team's P.A. announcer.

Former Lakers Mychal Thompson and Michael Cooper then took the court to say a few words about Tanter, who died at age 76 in September.

Mychal Thompson, left, and Michael Cooper honor the late Lawrence Tanter during a game between the Lakers and Jazz on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, in Los Angeles. Getty Images

"As much as you guys love him, we love him even more," said Thompson, who won two championships with the Lakers in 1987 and 1988 as Tanter served as the team's P.A. announcer.

Tanter was the voice of the Lakers during 10 NBA championships after being hired during the 1982-83 season.

The Los Angeles Lakers honor Lawrence Tanter outside Crypto.Com Arena on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, in Los Angeles, before a game against the Utah Jazz. NBAE via Getty Images

The Lakers also honored Tanter with a commemorative banner on Star Plaza outside of Crypto.com Arena before Monday's game. Fans were able to share personal messages and memories from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m.

Tanter suffered a a stroke in March before moving into an advisory role in June.

The Los Angeles Lakers honor Lawrence Tanter outside of Crypto.Com Arena before a game against the Utah Jazz in Los Angeles on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

"We are deeply saddened to share the news of the passing of legendary Lakers public address announcer Lawrence Tanter," the Lakers said in a statement in September.

"For 43 years, LT's voice served as the soundtrack to Lakers games at the arena. He will be remembered as a cherished member of the Lakers family."

#2570. Enzo Maresca has addressed the prospect of one day returning to manage in Italy as Manchester City await possible sanctions after being deemed guilty of breaching the Premier League's financial rules.

MATCH PREVIEW: Man City vs Napoli (UEFA Champions League)

Maresca, 46, was appointed City manager on June 29 on a three-year contract, replacing Pep Guardiola after 18 months at Chelsea that ended on New Year's Day.

The Italian oversaw a crucial period of rebuild at the Etihad Stadium over the summer, receiving significant financial backing from sporting director Hugo Viana to revamp the City dressing room after the Blues narrowly came up short to Arsenal in last season's Premier League title race.

After managing seven wins in his first seven Premier League games, Maresca and co have navigated a difficult run of results that has seen Manchester City lose three and draw one in their last four league outings, dropping to six points behind leaders Arsenal after 11 games.

The backdrop of the last two months of football has been set by an independent panel finding Manchester City guilty of breaching the Premier League's financial rules during 2009-18, with an appeal hearing slated for mid-December and possible sanctions to follow.

Despite backing Manchester City publicly in the wake of the guilty verdict, there have been serious questions raised over the future(s) of Maresca and his players should the club's appeal fail and the Blues go on to receive the harshest penalty, which could come in the form of expulsion from the Premier League.

Speaking in a press conference ahead of Tuesday's UEFA Champions League league phase clash against Napoli, Maresca was asked whether he would like to return to Italy as a manager after winning everything with City.

"Well, you never know what the future holds, do you? As I've said, I'm really, really happy being here, really happy here at the moment," the Italian said on Monday afternoon.

"I'm at a great club, wonderfully well-organised and after the last 17 years, they've only had three managers, which I think in comparison with what happens in Italy, this probably shows the continuity Man City have had."

Roberto Mancini, Manuel Pellegrini and Guardiola were the three managers who took charge of Manchester City between December 2009 and Maresca's appointment in the summer.

Mancini delivered City's first league title in 44 years in 2012, Pellegrini added another in 2014 and Guardiola won six Premier League titles during a decade in charge that included the treble in the historic 2022-23 campaign.

Quizzed about potentially being Maresca went on to clarify that he had been contacted by an Italian club between March and May, but insisted that he had never heard from Napoli president Aurelio De Laurentiis or any of the club's representatives.

The former Juventus, Fiorentina and Sampdoria midfielder first worked at City as manager of the Elite Development Squad, winning Premier League 2 in 2021, before returning as Guardiola's assistant for the treble-winning campaign.

He then won the EFL Championship with Leicester City in 2024, before claiming the UEFA Conference League and Club World Cup in his first season at Chelsea, where he was also named Premier League Manager of the Month twice, in September 2024 and November 2025.

City have fared better in Europe than in the Premier League of late, sitting seventh of 36 in the league phase after three wins from four, with their only defeat a 4-2 home loss to Paris Saint-Germain in October.

Allegri's Napoli arrive at the Etihad Stadium 27th in the standings and without nine players, although former City midfielder Kevin De Bruyne is part of their travelling squad for the game, with Scott McTominay's winner against Torino at the weekend having lifted them to eighth in Serie A.

#2568. Vikings Football and the Fine Art of Catastrophizing

In Week 11, Minnesota Vikings fans waited all day for Sunday Night. . .and almost immediately wished that they hadn't.

In what had been billed as one of the games of the year in the National Football League, the Vikings managed to hang with the San Francisco 49ers for about a quarter and a half before a late second-quarter touchdown pass from Brock Purdy and a pick-six from Kirk Cousins essentially ended things before halftime. The scoreboard said 35-10 at the end of the night, but it was over long before that.

Of course, the internet being what it is, there was much weeping and gnashing of teeth and rending of garments and those sorts of things. The euphoria that had washed over Vikings fans following the return of Kirk-a-Mania just a week prior had been swept away and replaced with the lament that Brian Flores' defense had been "exposed," and that teams around the league now had the "blueprint" to beat the league's top defense going forward.

Because that's the way things are now. Everything is either the greatest or the worst. Hell, sometimes things are both of those things simultaneously, somehow. Don't ask me how it happens, because I don't know. I'm fifty years old, and everything hurts. . .I can barely walk and chew gum at the same time, let alone reconcile those two things simultaneously.

But yes, the Niners put forth a very specific blueprint on Sunday night on how to beat the Vikings' defense. Step one of that blueprint is, apparently, "Start Brock Purdy at quarterback." That eliminates a lot of other teams from being able to emulate it. Honestly, that guy is operating on a level that pretty much no other quarterback in the league is currently operating on. I'll listen to an argument for Joe Burrow, but at this point that's just about it. He handled Flores' scheme in a way that nobody has in a very long time.

But even if the Niners did put a "blueprint" out there. . .so what?

Let me illustrate this with a slightly different example. If you play video games and you get stuck on a specific part of the game, you can pause the game or turn it off, head on over to YouTube, and find no shortage of videos of people showing you everything you need to do in order to get past that one particular spot you're having trouble with. You can probably even find four or five different people who will show you four or five different strategies to get through exactly the same map or boss or whatever it might be. You can watch all the videos your eyes can handle.

Eventually, however, you reach a point where you have to step away from the video, go back to your console, pick up your controller, and do the job yourself. And if your reflexes aren't fast enough or you hit the wrong button at the wrong time. . .well, that "blueprint" that you got from watching all those videos really doesn't do you a whole lot of good, does it? Teams can know what they have to do in order to beat the Vikings' defense all they want. How many teams can actually go out and do it?

The Vikings have lost three games so far this season. In two of those three losses, they were competitive until the late stages of the game, despite Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz looking like they had never actually seen a football before, never mind having any idea what the heck they were actually supposed to do with one. In the other one, they happened to run into the one team equipped. . .almost uniquely so. . .to beat them at what they do best. And if the Vikings should happen to meet up with that team again at some point, Flores has earned enough of my trust at this point for me to believe he's going to make enough changes to not let it happen again.

Now. . .while I can understand the disappointment after watching a game like Sunday night's loss, there's plenty of reason to be positive about the rest of the season. Am I crazy? Possibly, but that has nothing to do with football. Allow me to explain what I'm talking about as far as the Vikings are concerned.

The Vikings have seven games left on the schedule. Only two of those games will be played away from U.S. Bank Stadium. Those will be the Thursday Night Football game in Week 14 at New England and Week 17 at the New York Jets. The Patriots will be without Drake Maye and, as of now, are starting Tommy "In a Gadda" Devito at quarterback. The Jets. . .well, I was always taught that if you can't say anything nice. . .

The Vikings also only have two games remaining against teams with winning records the rest of the way. Both of them are against division opponents, and both of them are at home. Those will be on Sunday Night Football in Week 15 against Detroit (coming off a mini-bye following the New England game), and the regular-season finale against Chicago. The other three games are against Atlanta (currently 3-7), Carolina (currently 5-5), and Washington (currently 4-5-1).

According to PlayoffStatus.com, despite currently sitting behind both Detroit and Chicago in the NFC North, the Vikings have the inside track to both the NFC North title and the #2 seed in the NFC playoffs. They also have the second-highest odds of making the playoffs overall in the NFC at 93%. According to Tankathon, in terms of remaining strength of schedule, the Bears, Lions, and Packers rank #1, #5, and #7, respectively. The Vikings rank. . .#16. So the sledding is much tougher for the rest of the division, at least on paper, than it is for the purple.

You can make a pretty convincing argument that the Vikings could (should?) be favored in every game they play from here on out. The Lions and Bears play each other on Thanksgiving, so barring a tie, one of them is going to come out of Week 12 with a third loss. The Vikings have swept the Packers already, so Green Bay would need a minor miracle to overtake Minnesota for anything at this point.

The bottom line is that there's still plenty of football to be played, and while, yes, the loss to the Niners was painful to watch, it's not going to ruin the season or anything. There are adjustments to be made and, hopefully, this team will make them. Now it's time for them. . .and for us, as fans. . .to get up, dust ourselves off, and get ready for the last seven games of the year, starting with Kirkomecoming (if that's even a word, and if it's not, I just made it up) on Sunday afternoon at U.S. Bank Stadium.

#2567. Wolves 142, Nets 116: Defense Optional, Vibes Exceptional

Well, that was fun. If beatdowns and revenge against a former coworker are your thing, tonight's matchup was for you.

If they aren't, well, this was still a fun one.

On Monday night, the Minnesota Timberwolves dispatched the Brooklyn Nets 142-116. Minnesota did what it was supposed to do against one of the worst teams in the league as the Wolves look to put the harrowing memories of the Chicago Bulls game to rest.

Defense was clearly optional in this one, as both teams shot greater than 50% from the floor and over 40% from deep. Fortunately for us, what little defensive presence that did exist in this game came from the Timberwolves. Rudy Gobert and Joan Beringer had four steals apiece, and Beringer capped off his defensive showing with a whopping four blocks. All in all, this was one of the most complete showings that the Timberwolves have had all season.

With Thanksgiving around the corner, I'd like to take this opportunity to remind everyone that we, as Wolves fans, should be thankful that this team is good enough to consistently and authoritatively put away bad teams. Being at home for eight straight games surely helps team morale and rest, though this was a game that should have been, and was, definitively won. Not much room to poke holes in this performance. Even Rudy Gobert had a nice game!

While the Nets made a couple of runs in the second and fourth quarters to keep the game mildly interesting, there was never a sense of danger for the Wolves. They handled their business and look forward to the next matchup. Onward!

Here are a few of my takeaways from the game:

I'm not sure Anthony Edwards's prophetic line about how "we got Jaden McDaniels" is wholly accurate anymore. We might just have Kevin Durant. What a scintillating performance.

Already averaging career highs across all but one counting stat (blocks), McDaniels looks like there are no weak points left in his game. His midrange shots feel automatic. His threes are going in at a consistent clip amidst a steady volume of just over four attempts per game. Tonight, he made all four of his shots from distance, shot 12/16 from the floor as a whole, and set a new career high in points with 33 big ones.

Cap his performance off with 10 boards and six assists, and we might be looking at one of the best games of his career.

Most Wolves coverage this year has focused its attention on LaMelo Ball, Jonathan Kuminga, and the zany foibles of Gobert. In a sense, the silence around McDaniels speaks to his consistency and the greater expectations that the fanbase has for him. He's coming to work and doing his job every single night.

To say McDaniels might be the most important member of the team in the absence of Edwards is not an understatement. It certainly doesn't hurt that Jaden looks like Kevin Durant when he's playing, too. Silky. Smooth.

Ball has been in a statistical slump over the last few games – that much can't be argued. Tonight's performance was not much better in that regard, as he shot 6/16 from the floor, 2/10 from three, and only compiled three assists. At face value, this looks like a pedestrian performance.

Yet, I remain convinced that he is one of the most impactful players that the Timberwolves have on their roster. The highlights and deep shots do not necessarily tell the entire story of who he is as a player and how he impacts the game. What I'm saying is: we need to look beyond the box score to measure his effectiveness.

Yeah, I'm going to make a comparison to Rudy Gobert.

In the same vein as how Gobert's defensive impact cannot always be measured by things that show up on the stat sheet, Ball has that same effect on the offensive end. He is a master at manipulating defenses and drawing attention. His court vision is elite enough to make the right decision almost every time, and more often than not, he is putting his teammates in position to either make a play for themselves or to make a play for someone else.

Of course, hockey assists and other things like that are not counted in basketball. This is, however, why the Charlotte Hornets had such a crazy offensive rating last season when Ball stayed healthy. When he's on the court, everybody around him is better. It's not a coincidence. He carries all of the benefits of a heliocentric player with so few of the risks.

The shots will drop eventually. They may not be consistent, but that's okay! You live and die by those moments until Edwards returns. Until then, continue to appreciate everything that Ball has been offering this team in terms of flow, pace, and vision.

The sentiment of "they're all bad defenders" is no longer reserved for the Denver Nuggets. These Nets players have no defensive identity, or any identity at all.

It should come as no surprise that a team that lacks defensive intensity is one that is helmed by Julius Randle. Look, I get it, he did some great things during his time in Minnesota. He was an integral part of a team that made the Western Conference Finals. Randle had some great series, especially some standout ones on defense against the Los Angeles Lakers and Golden State Warriors, but that's about as far as any praise for defensive effort can go in his direction.

Randle had a great offensive showing tonight with 29 points on 11/16 from the floor. He also had his trademark five turnovers and finished with a team-worst -25 across his 35 minutes of play.

To be fair, the Nets are not a franchise that needs to be winning just yet. Still, when you have guys like Moritz Wagner blowing kisses to the away crowd while down by 20+ points, it's indicative of a team culture that does not take the game seriously. That comes from the top.

I do not think there should be any ill will towards Randle, though the resurgent team culture of the Timberwolves under LaMelo's leadership is exactly what the doctor ordered. Randle will get his stats while the Wolves accrue happiness points and wins. Seems like a good deal to me.

The Timberwolves take on the skidding Oklahoma City Thunder on Wednesday night at 6:30 PM. Catch that matchup on DAZN-MN and ESPN.

#2566. 'I could have yellow, pink, or green hair and I'll still play well' - Neymar hits back at 'arrogance' claims after bleached-hair Santos squad fall to Gremio

Neymar has hit back at claims of arrogance after he and several Santos team-mates arrived with bleached hair before suffering a frustrating 2-0 Brasileirao defeat to Gremio on Monday. The furious forward insisted hairstyles have nothing to do with football, blaming missed chances and a controversial penalty for the setback at Morumbi.

Neymar clashed with a reporter in the mixed zone after Santos fell 2-0 to relegation-threatened Gremio in front of around 45,000 fans in Sao Paulo. The No. 10, alongside Gabigol, Philippe Coutinho, Rodinei and Arthur, had sparked criticism by turning up with bleached hair. Francis Amuzu's 13th-minute opener and Martin Braithwaite's 76th-minute penalty sealed the visitors' victory, leaving Santos ninth on 50 points.

Despite dominating possession after falling behind early, Santos were repeatedly thwarted by Gremio goalkeeper Weverton, who denied Neymar, Everton Cebolinha and Gabigol.

Asked afterwards if the squad's bleached hair looked arrogant, Neymar said: "Who said that? They're completely wrong. Hair doesn't change anything. I dyed mine, and it changes absolutely nothing. Everyone has dyed their hair before, too. It has nothing to do with football!

"You saw that we played well. It came down to a small detail they capitalised on, on top of a poorly awarded penalty. Anyone who says something like that doesn't understand anything about football. They don't follow our day-to-day routine, they don't know what goes through our heads or how much pressure we put on ourselves."

He continued: "Of course we knew those kinds of comments would pop up, but those are opinions from people who don't understand football. It's part of it. Dyeing your hair changes nothing. We played very well. I could have yellow, pink, or green hair and I'll still play well in every game. Today, we just lacked a few minor adjustments and putting away our chances."

Renato Portaluppi's side struck first when Weverton's long ball found Carlos Vinicius to release Amuzu past Rodinei, before referee Ramon Abatti Abel awarded a penalty following a VAR review of Gonzalo Escobar's foul on Braithwaite. The win lifted Gremio to 15th on 41 points, overtaking Mirassol and pushing Corinthians into the bottom four.

Praising his side's display despite the result, Neymar added: "We played better than Gremio for practically the entire match. We put in a great performance, but there are days when the ball just won't go in.

"We ended up giving Gremio an opening. We knew it could happen on a single ball, on a counter-attack with Amuzu. It was a lapse on our part. With the experience our squad has, that's the kind of detail we can't afford to allow.

"They parked two buses at the back, and that made things tough. They're fighting to avoid relegation, so they're going to give their lives out there and run much harder. That makes things difficult. We played a great game. If we hadn't conceded that goal, it would have been a three-point match for us."

Santos remain in contention for Copa Libertadores qualification despite missing a chance to climb the table in front of their own supporters. They return to action next Sunday, November 29, visiting Vitoria at the Barradao in the penultimate round of the Brasileirao before hosting Botafogo on December 2. Gremio, meanwhile, now hold their Serie A survival in their own hands entering the final two rounds.

#2565. SEC plans to consider ejecting LSU on December 3

The supposed “chaos” in college sports could still result in the SEC kicking LSU out of the conference.

Via Mark Schlabach of ESPN, the conference plans to consider giving LSU the boot at a meeting on December 3.

The disclosure came in court papers filed Monday in connection with a legal battle arising from LSU’s placement of guard RJ Luis Jr. on the roster, after he played in preseason games for the Boston Celtics.

“The lawsuit seeks to protect the Conference’s ability to govern itself and to enforce the rules and policies its member universities have voluntarily adopted,” the SEC said in a statement. “The Conference maintains its right to associate only with institutions that meet its established standards and expectations of membership and that demonstrate appropriate institutional control of their athletics programs.”

The fight first emerged when the LSU football team considered adding to the roster players who had spots on 90-man NFL rosters in the offseason, training camp, and preseason. LSU eventually backed down.

The overriding question is whether players who have signed what are essentially tryout contract are “professional” players. And whether college athletes who are now being paid are not “professional.”

The entire dynamic arises from players making the strategic decision to pursue opportunities deemed to be more lucrative. College athletes in the high-revenue sports are essentially pro players. The fact that a small handful of players who have attempted to become pro players have chosen to return to college for business reasons creates a convenient — but disingenuous — talking point.

It’s easy, and phony, to frame it as “pro players” returning to college. They’re ALL pro players at this point, even if the NCAA and its members continue to covet an antitrust exemption that will allow them to restrict the amount of money the players can make, thereby diverting the finite booster funds toward the program, and the coaches.

It’s really that simple. The powers-that-be want to reduce the revenue stream for player, because that money can otherwise be funneled to the schools. But they won’t admit that, because that makes it harder to get public (and in turn political) support. It’s easier to frame it as “pro players playing in college sports.”

Again, they’re all professionals. As they should be. For decades. a corrupt system kept the players from getting their fair share. Now that they are, the fat cats who control college sports want to ensure that the players will get less. So that they can get more.

The fact that LSU isn’t participating in the ruse makes them an obvious target of the folks who are trying to perpetuate it. At some point, LSU should just stand up and tell the SEC to GFY.
