#2533. ‘I’m Fuming’ — NFL Analysts Ticked Off as Troy Aikman’s Steadfast War Against Analytics Rears Its Head During Bengals-Commanders on MNF

It's uncertain whether Pro Football Hall of Famer Troy Aikman will remain as the color commentator for ESPN's Monday Night Football after the 2026 NFL season. He remains without a contract extension as his five-year, $90 million deal expires after Super Bowl LXI in February 2027.

However, his recent performances from the booth aren't helping his cause to secure an extension. For example, NFL analysts pointed out Aikman's reaction during the fourth quarter of the Week 11 MNF game between the Washington Commanders and the visiting Cincinnati Bengals.

Down by one point, the Commanders faced a fourth-and-1 with around two and a half minutes left in regulation. Washington was at the Bengals' 24-yard line, and they could either kick the field goal or try to gain that yard and keep their drive going.

Commanders head coach Dan Quinn opted for the field goal, which Drew Stevens converted to give the home team a two-point lead. However, Aikman's declaration that it's difficult to argue with Quinn's decision irked football fans who tuned in to the game.

"I'm fuming. Every Monday night we have to listen to Buck and Aikman cry about coaches going for it on 4th down," Marcus Whitman said about Aikman's call. "They applauded the decision for them to kick the FG and are now doing everything they can to dance around the fact that Washington obviously should have gone for it."

Likewise, Derek Brown of FantasyPros sarcastically shared how Aikman's analysis usually sounds. "If you have heard one Troy Aikman broadcast, you've heard them all. Talk about the need to run the ball, toss shade at analytics, talk about Emmitt Smith, and use the phrase 'as good as anyone' as a quantifier."

Finally, NewsMax's Gerry Callahan, Cheesehead TV's Aaron Nagler, and Sports Radio 94WIP producer Buzz share the same thought but express it differently.

PREDICT THE NFL SEASON: PFN's Free NFL Playoff Predictor

"AIKMAN: You can't argue with the decision to kick the field goal. Really? Why can't you? Fourth and inches at the 23," Callahan tweeted. "And you decide to kick and you give Joe Burrow 2:20 to get a field goal? Yeah, you can argue with that, Troy. Shoulda gone for it."

"'You just can't argue with this decision.' Troy Aikman steadfastly refusing to join us in 2026," Nagler reacted.

"'You can't argue with this decision at 'all'—Troy Aikman on Dan Quinn taking the points on 4th and what appeared to be less than a full yard," Buzz commented. "To be clear, this decision puts the ball in the hands of the favorite to win league MVP with 2:30 to go, all 3 timeouts, and the 2-minute warning, only needing a field goal to win."

As Buzz and Callahan mentioned, going for it will help the Commanders extend their drive and take more time off from one of the leading candidates for this season's Most Valuable Player award. Instead, the field goal gave Washington the lead. Aikman has in the past expressed his opposition to analytics and had even argued that analytics could cost an HC his job.

Luckily for Aikman, the Commanders won 22-20 via another Stevens field goal after Evan McPherson briefly gave the Bengals the lead. But football fans will blame the three-time Super Bowl champion for ignoring analytics.

#2532. Recap: The lights in LA were too bright for Jazz

If you went to the middle of Main Street and even suggested that the Jazz would have one of their worst seasons through November, you would have likely been beaten to a pulp. But now, this is our reality. It's nearly comical how sonorously the wheel has fallen off the wagon.

In a game without Jaxson Hayes — Utah's starting frontcourt also watching in street clothes — the LA Lakers were in no room for any funny business, serving the Jazz their 16th loss of the year in a 109-94 finish. This game marked potentially the end of a season series (pending on NBA Cup consolidation matches), which is a bit silly to say in late November.

Will Hardy mentioned pregame that his goal was for the Jazz to limit their turnovers to under 12:

…The team proceeded to record eight turnovers in just the first quarter, and the Lakers scored nine points off of them. It felt like a one-sided battle right from the get-go, as LA toppled Utah by double digits after 12 minutes of action. Our only silver lining was Ace Bailey giving Walker Kessler a piece of him at the rim:

The Jazz have had trouble containing teams and building early advantages ever since their two-game winning streak, which has really struck them where it hurts when they start getting hot.

The second stint saw more of the same, leaving Utah hanging on by a thread. Utah dominated the paint and offensive rebounding, but there wasn't enough scoring (2-for-15 from deep) to allow them to close the gap. Rookie Darryn Peterson was the hot hand for the Jazz in the first half and led the way with 11 points for Utah. They got some impactful minutes from Kyle Filipowski, shooting an efficient 4-for-7 from the floor to rack up 10 points. It's always a pleasure to watch Flip get going, considering his fluctuating minutes and uncertain role on the roster.

The Jazz came out of halftime swinging, showcasing an elite defense anchored by Mo Bamba to come all the way back down 16. They took advantage of Luka Doncic, who had previously recorded four fouls at the half, attacking his side of the floor and giving him no space on the other end of the floor. Kyle Filipowski was completely cooking—he scored 6 of his points in the third period.

The Jazz struggled to spur a fourth-quarter run to build an advantage in the final outing. A 15-3 run by the Lakers gave them a double-digit lead in an instant. After exploding for 35 points in the third quarter, the offense finally dried up. The Jazz could not buy a bucket from deep. from three-point range. Svi Mykhailiuk (0-for-6 from three after hitting 10 triples on Sunday), Darryn Peterson (0-for-3), and Josh Okogie (0-for-3) have combined to go 0-for-12 from beyond the arc.

While Utah has only committed two more turnovers than Los Angeles (15 to 13), their mistakes have been live-ball turnovers that fuel the Lakers' running game. Luka stopper Josh Green fouled out, forcing Utah into heavy minutes for an already depleted rotation.

In his rookie year, it seemed like Kyle Filipowski was destined to be our mini-Lauri Markkanen. The size, the footwork, the athleticism, the jump shot—it was too good to be true. Then, Flip gradually fell out of the rotation over the next two seasons, and the emergence of Mo Bamba seemed to bury him for good. But with the Jazz being extra shorthanded, Kyle Filipowski finally got his shine.

He did most of his damage inside the restricted area, mixing rim finishes with a three-pointer and three assists while limiting turnovers to just one. Will Hardy gave him the Jusuf Nurkic playbook and he took that role with ease. Passing and handling bigs make the offense run with no squeaks.

The first half was as atrocious as you could ask for. The 10 turnovers in the first half had the Jazz playing uphill all night long. The Lakers turned Utah's live-ball mistakes into 18 points off turnovers and fueled a massive 26–9 fast-break advantage late in the fourth quarter. JJ Redick's aggressive defensive pressure and zone looks disrupted the Jazz's style of play.

The lack of defensive discipline was also a major concern—it's mind-blowing how frequently the Jazz put opponents into the bonus early in quarters. Utah sits in the bottom 10 in opponent free-throw rate and averages roughly 23–24 personal fouls per game. Giving away free points at the line prevents Utah from setting their half-court defense and compounds their own poor free-throw shooting (ranking 28th in the NBA in FT%).

The stagnant iso-ball continues to be the worst offensive set this team has ever run. When shots stop falling or defenses turn up the physicality, Utah abandons ball movement. Too many possessions devolve into zero- or one-pass isolations late in the shot clock.

The fourth quarter encapsulated all three of these weaknesses into 12 minutes of ugly basketball. The great defense in the third quarter was wasted the moment they took their foot off the gas.

Utah drops to 3-16 with this loss and lines up their next matchup in Denver on Thursday night, marking the first matchup between these two teams.

#2531. Which team needs Tarik Skubal the most? Ranking the suitors for the best free agent available

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As we emerge from the recent General Manager Meetings and move toward the expected Dec. 1 lockout of the players by MLB owners, we might see an accelerated pace of activity soon. The most tantalizing possibility is that ace and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, the undisputed top talent on the free agent market this winter, will sign before the sport shuts down for an indeterminate amount of time.

The decorated lefty, who soon turns 30, is our No. 1 free agent of the 2026-27 class, and it's not an especially close call. Here's part of our write-up:

"Excluding Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who was a special case as a Japanese star with no MLB track record, Skubal is the best starting pitcher to hit free agency since Gerrit Cole in 2019. He showed few long-lasting effects from the NanoScope elbow surgery in May and remains a capital-A Ace with terrific surface stats and under-the-hood performance indicators. Skubal brings four swing-and-miss pitches to the table (four-seamer, changeup, slider, curveball), a near MLB-best ability to limit exit velocity, and elite strike-throwing ability (MLB's third-lowest walk rate since 2023). Build an ace starter in a lab and he would look a lot like Skubal. He'll play the entire 2027 season at age 30, and given the things teams can do with pitchers these days, Skubal figures to remain a frontline starter for most of a long-term contract. He's the only true balance-of-power player available in free agency this offseason. Skubal can swing a division race and a postseason series all by himself."

Will he set the record for the biggest contract ever signed by a pitcher? Will Skubal fetch the highest average annual salary for a pitcher? Will he top $400 million? Those are all reasonable questions to ask. First, though, there's a question to be asked about the teams that are already pursuing him the most vigorously. That question is, which team needs him the most? We're restricting our discussion to the five teams that have been most reliably linked to Skubal so far this offseason. We're already hearing reports of surprise teams, and it's always possible a surprise late bidder will enter the fray and even win his signature, but for now, these five clubs are the favorites. This, then, is an ordering of those teams based on which desperately needs a talent like Skubal in order to reach their goals in 2027 and beyond. Let's get to it, in order from "needs him the most" to "needs him but not as urgently as the teams ahead of them" …

The Cubs are in contention mode and in need of roster improvements if they're going to run down the world champion Milwaukee Brewers in the National League Central. The rotation is without question the most pressing need for Chicago. Shota Imanaga, Matthew Boyd, David Peterson, and deadline acquisition Clay Holmes are all free agents. Justin Steele hasn't taken the mound at the big-league level since early in the 2025 season thanks to UCL surgery and a halting recovery process. While he's expected to be ready for 2027, he's not exactly a known quantity right now. Young upsider Cade Horton may not be back until midseason after undergoing Tommy John surgery, and Ben Brown, who recently had neck surgery, may be on a similar timeline. So, yes, the Cubs need a lot of rotation help, and Skubal would give them the true frontline ace they'd lack even if everyone were healthy. Unfortunately for the Cubs fans, it sounds like the Ricketts aren't willing to be truly competitive for his services.

Coming off the grave disappointments of 2026, the Mets could certainly use a headline-grabbing addition to improve their chances in 2027 and inspire a surely disaffected fan base. Beyond that, the Mets need more starting pitching to accompany promising young Nolan McLean. Christian Scott seems like a lock, but he doesn't project as a frontliner. They have some depth options for the back end, but they need a true needle-mover like Skubal at the very front. That's especially the case in what figures to be a hotly competitive NL East in 2027. Thus far, David Stearns and owner Steve Cohen sound committed to making a good-faith run at Skubal.

The Padres have a lot of work to do if they're going to earn a fourth straight playoff appearance. Speaking of which, the rotation is crying out for help right about now. They lost Dylan Cease to free agency last winter, and this time Michael King may be bound elsewhere, too. The Pads declined their club option on Nick Pivetta, and while they hope to bring him back on more favorable terms, there's no guarantee they'll be able to do that. Yes, Joe Musgrove will be back, but how much can he give them and how effective will he be? They'll need even more help if Adrian Morejon, a lockdown bulk reliever and possible starter-conversion project, signs elsewhere. Skubal's made to order, and signing the top talent on the market would be a strong signal by new owners José E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones that the team's recent tradition of spending and contending won't be fading away.

The Dodgers self-evidently needed Skubal enough to acquire him from the Detroit Tigers leading up to the deadline and do so at significant cost. On paper, the Dodgers aren't as desperate for rotation help as the teams ahead of them on this list, but there's still a need. Yoshinobu Yamamoto is a certifiable ace, but behind him Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow are established health and durability risks. Shohei Ohtani is something of an unknown, at least insofar as his pitching is concerned right now, and thus far Roki Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan have not proved worthy of being relied upon. One can squint and see the Dodgers' current championship window closing in the reasonably near future, which means that's all the more reason to push the chips in now. Retaining the elite services of Skubal would greatly aid the cause in 2027.

Eyeball a rotation that already includes Dylan Cease, José Soriano, and Trey Yesavage, and you might think it doesn't need much more. And maybe it doesn't. As a matter of principle, though, any team with contending aspirations should be interested in a top-shelf ace when he hits the market. The Jays, who in recent years have invested in the roster at commendable levels, are no doubt dreaming of a Skubal-Cease one-two punch that would be the envy of, oh, every other team in baseball. There's also depth to think about. In particular, Cody Ponce is a bit of an unknown coming off knee surgery that ended his 2026 season in the middle of his first start. Addressing the offense probably should be more of a priority for the Jays this winter, but, again, it's Tarik Skubal, and the likes of Tarik Skubal make any team better.

#2529. Lakers surge in fourth quarter to beat Jazz, win for 11th time in 12 games

It took some work for the Lakers to win Monday night against the Utah Jazz.

It took playing as a whole unit, and it took a strong defensive effort when the offense struggled.

Five players scored in double figures, and the Lakers needed every bit of their contributions to pull off a 109-94 win at Crypto.com Arena.

Luka Doncic led the Lakers with 28 points, but he was just eight for 24 from the field and three for 14 from three-point range.

Read more: Walker Kessler's first three-pointer as a Laker sparks resurgent second half

Walker Kessler had a double-double with 10 points and 12 rebounds to go along with two blocks. Jake LaRavia had a double-double with 15 points and 10 rebounds. Matisse Thybulle scored 14 points and Collin Sexton had 12 points off the bench.

The Lakers shot 43% from the field and just 29% from three-point range. But they held the Jazz (3-16) to just 32% shooting from the field in the fourth quarter, outscoring them 31-17.

"I would say that's pretty good defense," Kessler said. "I think our transition defense has gotten better, which is nice to see. Our limiting second-chance points has gotten better. Obviously, we can still improve on that. We're kind of struggling right now with open threes, but I feel like, you know, we had a kind of a tough stretch where they kind of came back in the second half. ... I think we're trending upwards and that's all you want to see."

Despite their shooting struggles, the Jazz threatened to beat the Lakers for the second time in less than a week before a fourth-quarter surge helped the Lakers pull away. The group of Sexton, Thybulle, LaRavia, Kessler and Quentin Grimes started the fourth quarter and helped the Lakers build a 13-point lead.

By the time Doncic returned to the game with 6:01 left, the Lakers led 95-84 and were on their way to their 11th win in 12 games.

Lakers star Luka Doncic controls the ball in front of Utah Jazz forward Kyle Filipowski during the first quarter Monday. (Ronaldo Bolaños / Los Angeles Times)

"I think the fourth quarter determines a lot of the game," Sexton said. "And at the end of the day, we got to come out with that juice, with that fire. And I feel like the last couple games, we've been doing that. I think a big part of it is just that start. And I think that whoever starts that fourth quarter has to set the tone for the rest of the game. So, I think we got to try to change the flow, change the way the game was going."

Now the Lakers prepare to face the Spurs in San Antonio on Friday in an NBA Cup group play showdown.

The teams are tied for the best record in the NBA at 15-3. They also have the league's biggest stars in Doncic and Victor Wembanyama for the Spurs.

"We're going to prepare for it the same way we prepare for every other game and we're going to game plan the same way we have and we're going to go in there and play the same way that we've been doing," LaRavia said. "So, we got three days, obviously, to kind of rest and recover and game plan for this game on Friday, 'cause you're right, it is a big game."

Bob Iger, far left, sits next to Jeanie Buss and Josh Kushner, second right, sits next to Rob Pelinka during Monday's game. Kushner and Iger have entered into an agreement with Lakers owner Mark Walter to buy the team. (Ronaldo Bolaños / Los Angeles Times)

Austin Reaves missed his fifth straight game with a left heel bruise, but he is making progress, coach JJ Redick said. Reaves was able to participate in the Lakers' stay-ready-games on Monday.

"We want to be consistent with our RTP [return to play] stuff," Redick said. "I think today was a big step just in terms of getting a stay-ready game in. And he played great, moved great. I think we're optimistic for the rest of this week going forward."

The annual GM Meetings came and went last week with two significant transactions. Teams are calling the Rangers about left-hander MacKenzie Gore, who is a year away from free agency, according to The Athletic. There is some reluctance to trade for players with only one year of control because games could be lost to a work stoppage next year, but pitching is so in-demand that at least some clubs are exploring a deal for Gore.

Now 27, Gore is one of only six pitchers to make at least 30 starts in each of the last three years. His under-the-hood numbers (3.87 FIP and 4.19 expected ERA) were much better than his 4.58 actual ERA, plus he has long been considered to have untapped upside. Gore will give you innings, at minimum, and there's a chance his best days are ahead of him.

The Vikings defence had not conceded more than 23 points in a game this season, but the 49ers offence outsmarted them in front of 85,612 fans in Mexico City.

The 49ers scored four touchdowns in the first half - two by George Kittle - before running out 35-10 winners.

Mike Evans returned after missing three games with an Achilles problem to finish with 109 receiving yards and a touchdown.

With the game played at high altitude - about 7,220ft (2,240m) above sea level - some players used oxygen masks on the sidelines.

#2524. Spurs overcome slow start in Sacramento for eighth road win of the season

The short-staffed San Antonio Spurs handled the Kings in Sacramento, remaining perfect on the road, and they continue to allow the fewest points average in the Western Conference (105.4). It was the third of four matchups this season, and the Spurs did not get this one easy, while Stephon Castle did lots of the heavy lifting and the background players got extra burn.

After the game, coach Mitch Johnson gave props to some of the role players for staying ready. "This is what character is. This is what a program is, in terms of you don't necessarily know when and there's a lot of un-controllables throughout a long season…"

Despite the Kings' abysmal record, they had shown more fight recently, testing the Los Angeles Lakers in a close loss and handing the Boston Celtics their third-straight loss. Yet their luck wasn't the same on Monday as the Spurs were likely on high alert for a trap game. Domantas Sabonis was a force in the lane, but this was watered down by the squad's relentless hustle, and Castle later caused him to pick up his sixth foul, forcing him to sit.

It took some time for the Spurs to get settled as they had their worst opening quarter of the season (24 percent shooting). Aside from not having much horse power early, the horde did not have its usual synchronicity as they tried to key in on movement inside the lane.

Then Julian Champagnie stepped up, shooting the team out of the slump in the second quarter with five 3-pointers, and that breathed life into them on the other end. They finished the period, holding the hosts to 39.8 percent shooting and claimed a nine-point lead going into halftime after being down by a dozen points.

The Spurs were still still having trouble after the break forcing Darius Acuff Jr to his off-hand, yet the third quarter subsequently turned into the Castle and Devin Vassell show. They buried five 3-pointers, and Castle got the step on defenders. The rest of the team followed their lead, but the Kings had one run left in them, cutting the lead to eight points as the Spurs were cold to start the fourth.

It took a late surge before the Spurs could put the squeeze on them, and Castle plus Luke Kornet's fingerprints were all over it.

The Spurs won 123-107, extending their streak to three with one game left on their brief road trip.

Castle and Vassell were pressing early, making only two of their first 13 shots. They compensated for it by keeping their teammates involved and rebounding. Castle eventually found his forms and took the reins as the primary shot creator. He had his third double-double of the season of 28 points, 11 assists and eight rebounds plus set the tone with his defense, particularly, not picking up any cheap fouls. Vassell finished with 16 points, six rebounds and two assists.

The second quarter was the decisive moment of the game as the Spurs outscored them by 18 points (41-23) and logged a monstrous 157.7 offensive rating. Champagnie had 17 of his 22 points in that period.

The Spurs are usually one of the top transition teams in the league, and they only generated a few easy baskets as they didn't push the pace much. They made up for it with their pursuit of rebounds, which turned into 26 second-chance points, their most of the season. Kornet deserves most of the credit for those (9).

Without Wemby, the front-line rotation was Kornet and Tarris Reed Jr., so defensive communication was not the same, also relying more often on drop coverage and the Kings spent a good chunk of the game attacking without fear. Additionally, without Wemby's screening, Sacramento's low man only guarded one player instead of two on pick-and-roll plays. This made it a little harder for Castle to score at close range.

It takes a lot of talent to get things done in the NBA, and that still doesn't guarantee wins, so any victory with three starters missing matters. Forget that the Kings' record was 2-14 going into this game; there are still guys with pride on that team, and their eyes probably lit up when they saw the absences on the San Antonio side. They went for it and had the Spurs in a tough game for most of the first half. The Spurs were still able to score 127.3 points per 100 possessions, good enough for the 86th percentile. Not one Spur having more than two turnovers played a part in that.

Before this game, 19 3-pointers was the most the Kings had allowed this season. The Spurs had 16 and none came after the third quarter.

On a screen-roll play, Castle lobbed it perfectly to Kornet for a finish through contact.

#2523. ‘Are You Kidding Me?’ ‘This Is Bad’ — NFL Fans Question Chargers HC Jim Harbaugh After He Looks to Staff for Answers In a Press Conference

A disastrous season for the Los Angeles Chargers continued in Week 11. After falling to a 27-24 defeat at the hands of the New York Jets, the Chargers became the only home team to lose this week. And if that wasn't enough, one exchange from Jim Harbaugh after the game raised even more eyebrows.

It's safe to say that any momentum garnered from their first win of the season the week prior vanished into smoke the minute the Chargers lost to the Jets at home.

With that in mind, the interaction in question between Harbaugh and the media was eye-opening for a lot of fans.

The interaction saw a reporter ask him who was wearing the green dot on the field to ensure necessary adjustments were being made. However, Harbaugh appeared unsure about the situation, unsure about which player had it.

The green dot on the helmet typically signifies the player on the field who has a headpiece and a direct line of communication with the coaches to get the play calls and relay the information to others on the field.

But Harbaugh, as the head coach, did not know who that was for the Chargers, as he asked around with his staff to get the right answer. The exchange drew criticism on social media and provided some more insight into everything that has gone wrong this year.

One fan pointed out, "It's very odd to me how little he actually knows about how his team is run."

#2521. Why Potts swapped West Ham for Club Brugge after 16 years

When Liverpool visit Club Brugge on Wednesday they are likely to come up against English midfielder Freddie Potts.

The 23-year-old ended a 16-year association with West Ham in the summer to join the Belgian champions for an undisclosed fee.

And he has started every game, bar one missed through suspension, in all competitions.

After losing to Aston Villa in the Champions League, they have defeated Inter Milan, Lens and PSV.

"It really is a dream because you hear the music and then you see your family in the stands and you remember all the times that you watched Champions League on TV," Potts told BBC Radio 5 Live's Euro Leagues Show.

"You think of all the memories that you make watching it and to be playing in it now is something that every kid dreams of."

Potts' whole life had been based around West Ham. He had been with the club since the age of six and his father Steve, who made 506 appearances for the Hammers, is a first-team coach.

Potts Jr played 28 times for West Ham, with 25 of them coming last season as they were relegated from the Premier League.

He also had loan spells with Wycombe in League One and Portsmouth in the Championship.

"In pre-season my minutes with West Ham were limited, they weren't as much as I wanted and then I spoke with my agent and said 'let's explore options because this season I'm 22, turning 23'," Potts said.

"It's a massive part of my career and I wanted to play. The opportunity of Club Brugge came along with Champions League football, the best club in Belgium and it was an opportunity I couldn't really turn down with how my minutes were going down with West Ham.

"I grew up in the area, going to the stadium watching the games. It was always going to be a tough decision but it was something that I had to do for my career.

"It was an emotional decision because it had to be made quite quickly. It's been the right decision for me and so far I'm enjoying it, I'm loving life here."

Club Brugge won the Belgian title last season and are second, just one point behind leaders Union Saint-Gilloise this campaign.

"It's a physical league," said Potts. "My running and physical stats have been higher than they've ever been. It's a demanding league in that way.

"Club Brugge demands a lot, from winning the ball back and going man for man in the press. And your responsibility off the ball is something that you have to take really seriously."

Freddie Potts on leaving West Ham, life in Belgium and beating Inter Milan

Potts says he has not started to learn French or Flemish and that team talks are done in English, with the side managed by Croat Ivan Leko.

And he revealed he has a lifelong history with the city.

"The whole move itself is funny because we used to visit Brugge when I was a kid," he said.

"We used to come around Christmas, so my family all know the city. And now I'm here they come out as much as they can.

"It's a great city with a lot of culture. It's brilliant. You won't find many places like it."

#2517. NBA MVP Rankings: Luka Dončić, Victor Wembanyama in a two-horse race; Stephen Curry's absence speaks volumes

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We're nearly a month into the 2026-27 NBA season, and while some people say it's too early to start talking about MVP, we are not among those people.

Right now, it's a clear two-horse race: Luka Doncic or Victor Wembanyama? There is a real split on this. Here's where I stand as of Tuesday, Nov. 17.

The Luka Dončić we're watching right now isn't just the best offensive player in the world. He might be the best in history. Nobody has ever put up anything close to the numbers he is charting at the moment: 39 points per game with seven assists, seven boards, nearly two steals and a positively scorching 66.0 TS%, the latter being a number even the great Stephen Curry has only bested twice in his career.

It's early, sure. Dončić isn't likely to keep making 3s at this rate for an entire season, and indeed we've seen some slippage of late (35% over his last four, if you really want to split hairs), but his volume remains, with 4.5 makes a night over that stretch. Dončić remains on track to break Curry's single-season record of 402 3-pointers, and he's done more off-ball shooting than in the past.

Throw in more transition production and a 53% midrange conversion rate, per Cleaning The Glass, and you're seeing a more diverse scorer, which is to say this isn't just a guy who has started off hot on his step-back 3s (though this is a major factor, too, of course), but a guy piercing defenses from more spots with different shots. If Dončić could actually be any harder to guard than he has been in the past, we're seeing it this season.

He's also defending. His 23 steals rank sixth league-wide. Only two players have recovered more defensive loose balls than his eight. Only one has taken more charges than his four. With Dončić as the primary defender, shooters are converting just 36.7% of their shots against a 45.1 expected FG%; that minus-8.6 is the fourth-largest discrepancy among all players who've contested at least 150 shots.

Most importantly, the Lakers are 12-2 and tied with the Spurs atop the Western Conference. The Lakers rank as the league's top offense with a rating that balloons to 129.2 points per 100 possessions (which would be an NBA record by a long shot) with Dončić on, and a net rating, as illustrated below, that falls off a cliff when he sits.

Look, if you have Wembanyama ahead of Dončić in the MVP race a month into the season, nobody is going to argue much with you. The oddsmakers slightly favor Wembanyama (+110 at FanDuel; Dončić is +140), who, as you'll see below, has what would qualify as a potentially unanimous case in most years. But this isn't most years. We got a dude averaging nearly 40 points for a No. 1 seed that nobody expected to be a No. 1 seed. Until one of those things changes, it's hard for me to go against Dončić.

If you think Dončić's plus-35.5 on/off split (it's actually plus-32.2 without filtering for garbage time) is crazy, have a look at Wembanyama's number.

Victor Wembanyama's impact this season has been another level. Spurs are +42.6 points per 100 possessions with Wemby on the court than off it, according to @cleantheglass. Small sample but other-worldly. Lakers star Luka Dončić is at +35.5 pts/100 poss.Both numbers are better… pic.twitter.com/0GJCFFmZ5K

Yes, you're reading that right. The Spurs, for all their supportive talent, fall by 42.6 points per 100 possessions when Wembanyama leaves the court (plus-29.2 on vs. minus-13.3 off), per Cleaning the Glass. By comparison, the best on/off split that Nikola Jokić has ever recorded is plus-24.8. Curry's best is plus-21.3. LeBron James' is plus-17.8. Go down that list and look at the most impactful on-off splits those guys have ever posted. Wembanyama is in another galaxy.

And it's important to note that Wembanyama plays on a great team, as all these guys in the graphic have. The fact that there is still so much difference between when Wembanyama is on the court and when he isn't, even in a small sample, is honestly difficult to comprehend. San Antonio's three-guard lineup was supposed to be an experiment, but it's hard to know if Dylan Harper, De'Aaron Fox and Stephon Castle truly optimize one another or if Wembanyama is enough to make any lineup dominant in spite of traditional issues (like none of those three being a true shooter).

Wembanyama is the best defensive player on the planet by an immeasurable amount. Even the stats don't do it justice. He's on pace for north of 350 blocks, a number only four players (Elmore Smith, Mark Eaton, Manute Bol and Hakeem Olajuwon) have eclipsed since blocks became an official stat in 1973, and still it's just as much, if not more, about the shots he deters scorers from even attempting.

And why would they? Scorers are making just 33.6% of their shots when Wembanyama is the nearest defender, a 17% drop from their expected 50.4%. That also leads the league among all players who've defended at least 120 shots, and again, it fails to fully capture his defensive dominance.

The fact that we've gotten this far without talking about Wembanyama's offense, as if it's a mere afterthought for a guy to be averaging 28.6 points and 11.6 rebounds in under 30 minutes a night. Wembanyama is figuring out his hot spots, prioritizing closer-to-the-basket positioning where he is a skyscraper among regular NBA buildings. He's taking two more paint shots per game than he did last season; 43% of his shots are coming from inside four feet, per Cleaning the Glass, up from 38% last season, and his 4.6 dunks per game (up from 2.7 last year) have him on pace to shatter Rudy Gobert's single-season record of 306.

If I had to guess, Wembanyama's production is more sustainable than Dončić's. It's hard to imagine Dončić not hitting a rough patch from 3, and he's almost certainly not going to keep scoring 39 points per game. He'll be over 35 points per game when everything is said and done because that's what the Lakers need from him, but there's a burnout factor while Wembanyama is kind of cruising to these numbers, and the defensive impact is as natural as breathing. My gut says Wembanyama will be a clearer MVP favorite by Christmas.

Assuming Dončić and Wembanyama each get to the mandated 65 games, everyone else is playing for third place at the moment. Which is crazy given the seasons some of the following names are having.

One of two players averaging at least 22 points, nine rebounds and seven assists, and the only player to be leading his team in all three categories. The Rockets are 11-4 with the No. 2 offense and Sengun is the center of it all.

Tatum is averaging his normal 26.5 points per game. The shooting efficiency still hasn't come around, but he is an absolute quarterback on this Celtics team. He draws the doubles, and his 35.1% assist rate, per CTG, is a career high by a mile. The Celtics, for my money, are the best team in the East.

Cunningham is, once again, doing everything for the Pistons, who have been without Jalen Duren for all but the first four games and are still a top-three East seed. The 3-point shooting is down, but that's splitting hairs. This guy is shot-creating machine and, as forceful as he plays, he makes it look as smooth as anyone in the league.

Here come the Heat, who have won five straight games, with the last three wins coming over the Cavaliers, Pistons and Rockets. Antetokounmpo is averaging 28.3/12.5/5.2 with 1.3 blocks per game on 60% shooting. He's on fire from the midrange as the Heat are exploiting the soft spots in all the drop coverage they're facing.

Gilgeous-Alexander has so much on his plate that it actually creates a clearer path to a third straight MVP if he can somehow lift Oklahoma City above all these injuries. He's trying. The Thunder are 9-5 and he's getting his 30.9 points per game, but his 58.7 true-shooting is down considerably, which makes sense as he has to force tougher shots now with fewer weapons around him.

Curry's value can perhaps be felt most in his absence. The Warriors have lost three straight since he went out with a torn oblique, the last two by 59 points. The Warriors have outscored opponents by 13.5 points per 100 possessions with Curry on the floor this season and have been outscored by 8.3 points per 100 possessions without him. Along with Yaxel Lendeborg, who's being asked as a rookie to carry an impossibly heavy weight without Curry, Curry remains the only real lifeblood of a team that is still shockingly lifeless without him.

#2516. Jake Bauers signs four-year, $58 million deal with Red Sox after helping lead Brewers to World Series

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Boston Red Sox have made the offseason's first major free agent signing. The Red Sox and first baseman Jake Bauers have agreed to a four-year contract worth a reported $58 million, the team announced on Tuesday.

Bauers, 31, broke out with the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers this past season, authoring a .266/.389/.484 batting line with 26 home runs that more than doubled his previous career high (12). He was named the NLCS MVP during Milwaukee's title run thanks to a 4 for 14 (.286) effort. Bauers drove in seven runs in the four-game sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers.

The Red Sox desperately needed a power bat and certainly added one with Bauers. Their 163 home runs this past season were the fifth fewest in baseball and three players -- Wilyer Abreu, Willson Contreras and Jarren Duran -- accounted for 71 of those 163 home runs. Boston's lineup figures to look something like this with Bauers now added:

That leaves Duran without a full-time position and makes a trade or even a non-tender more likely. Franklin Arias, one of the very best prospects in the minors, could debut early next season and wrestle the shortstop job away from Story. POBO Craig Breslow recently said Story is not locked in as the team's starting shortstop.

We ranked Bauers as the 12th-best free agent available this offseason, and the seventh-best position player free agent. Here's our write-up:

Rake Bauers (finally) lived up to the nickname this year and carried it over into the postseason, particularly during the NLCS. Long an exit velocity and hard-hit rate darling, Bauers fully tapped into his power in 2026 thanks to a more open stance and moving back in the box and further off the plate. That allowed him to see the ball better and get his bat into the hitting position on time more consistently. I'm not 100% sold on those adjustments solving his career-long issues with lefties, though at least there is a tangible reason to believe in his great left-on-left performance this season. Bauers can be an adventure in the field (he has played outfield in the past) and he just turned 31. A few teams will look for the next Jake Bauers rather than pay the actual Jake Bauers.

The Brewers tendered Bauers the $23.15 million qualifying offer and will receive a 2027 compensation draft pick after the first round because the contract exceeds $50 million. Because they paid the competitive balance tax, the Red Sox will forfeit their second- and fifth-highest 2027 draft picks, plus $1 million in bonus pool money for the 2027 international signing period, to sign Bauers.

Milwaukee could turn to Tyler Black and Andrew Vaughn at first base next season. Andrew Fischer, the No. 20 overall pick in the 2025 draft, slugged 48 home runs in the minors this summer and reached Double-A. He is the long-term solution at first base but is likely a year away from the big leagues. The Brewers could bring in a stopgap first baseman if they're not sold on Black.

The Red Sox went 87-75 this past season and were the second wild card team. They were swept by the rival New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series and scored only two runs in the two games.

#2512. Yankees' David Bednar, Twins' Ryan Jeffers accept qualifying offer, six others reject $23.15 million QO

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Two players have accepted this year's one-year, $23.15 million qualifying offer prior to Tuesday's 4 p.m. ET. deadline, and six others have declined the QO. David Bednar (Yankees) and Ryan Jeffers (Twins) are returning to their teams, for the 2027 season, while Randy Arozarena (Mariners),  Brandon Lowe (Pirates), Adrian Morejon (Padres), Trevor Rogers (Orioles), and Seiya Suzuki (Cubs) are all hitting the market.

An eighth free agent, Jake Bauers, also received the QO. He agreed to a four-year, $58 million contract with the Red Sox this past weekend. Effectively, Bauers declined the QO. Because they paid CBT in 2026, the Red Sox will surrender their second- and fifth-highest 2027 draft picks, plus $1 million in 2027 international bonus pool money, to sign Bauers. The Brewers, as a revenue-sharing receiver, will receive a compensation draft pick after the first round because the contract exceeds $50 million.

The five unsigned free agents who rejected the QO are now tied to draft pick compensation. Their former teams will receive a draft pick if they sign elsewhere, and their new teams will be docked a draft pick and potentially international bonus pool money to sign them. The exact compensation depends on the team's revenue sharing and competitive balance tax (CBT) status.

Here is draft pick compensation the former teams will receive if the seven qualified free agents change teams:

Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round) if contract under $50M; pick after first round if over $50M

Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round) if contract under $50M; pick after first round if over $50M

Pick after competitive balance round B (before third round) if contract under $50M; pick after first round if over $50M

CBT payors, like the Red Sox, will forfeit their second- and fifth-highest 2027 draft picks, plus $1 million in 2027 international bonus pool money, to sign a qualified free agent. Teams that receive revenue sharing will surrender their third-highest 2027 draft pick. All other teams will surrender their second-highest 2027 draft pick and $500,000 in 2027 international bonus pool money.

It must be noted that declining the QO does not mean the free agent can not return to his former team. The two sides could still work out a contract of any size and any length, including one worth less than QO, though that is very unlikely. Zac Gallen, Michael King, and Kyle Schwarber rejected the QO last offseason and then later re-signed with their teams.

Free agents must meet certain criteria to be eligible for the QO. Players cannot have received the QO previously and they must have spent the most recent season with one team, meaning anyone traded in-season is ineligible. The Dodgers could not give Tarik Skubal, far and away the offseason's best free agent, the QO following his midseason acquisition.

The QO is set at the average of the top 125 salaries in the most recent season and that is salaries only, not total compensation. For example, the Yankees paid Cody Bellinger a $20 million signing bonus and a $32.5 million salary in 2026. Only the $32.5 million counts toward the QO calculation. This QO was worth a record $23.15 million this winter.

The current QO system replaced the old free-agent arbitration system in 2012 and will remain in effect this offseason. The upcoming collective bargaining agreement could change the QO system, if not eliminate it entirely. Entering the offseason, just 18 of the 157 free agents to receive the QO accepted it. That count is now at 20 of 165.

One of the more effective closers in baseball last season, Bednar closed down 35 of 39 save chances with a 2.47 ERA, 1.04 WHIP and 76 strikeouts in 69 ⅓ innings. Having him back on board means the Yankees don't need to find a new closer and can look instead to shore up the bridge to the ninth as needed.

There had been talk that Jeffers wanted to stay with the Twins but that he'd decline the QO and then negotiate a long-term deal. There's still room to reach an extension, of course, but he now doesn't have any leverage from outside offers. It's a big win for the Twins, with Jeffers resuming his role as the everyday catcher and Victor Caratini serving as the primary backup.

Jeffers hit .256/.353/.461 (127 OPS+) with 14 homers and 56 RBI is only 92 games last season. He's been one of the most productive offensive catchers in baseball over the course of the last four seasons, when healthy.

#2511. Pictures: Fresh look at Barcelona’s leaked home kit for the 2027/28 season

Barcelona's 2027/28 home kit has emerged in a fresh batch of images, offering fans a closer look at Nike's plans to bring back a more traditional Blaugrana design. '

The latest photographs, published by kit specialists Footy Headlines, show a replica based on the expected design, featuring numerous narrow blue and maroon stripes, darker colours and contrasting yellow details.

The shirt is expected to be officially released in early summer 2027.

The design will be a noticeable departure from the more experimental approach associated with Barcelona's leaked 2027/28 third kit, which draws inspiration from Catalonia's traditional Correfoc celebrations.

Instead, Nike appears to be returning to the club's familiar home-shirt identity, with a contemporary interpretation of its historic colours.

Leaked design of Barcelona's home kit for the 2027/28 season. (Source: Footy Headlines)

The most distinctive feature of the Barcelona 2027/28 home kit is its traditional vertical stripe pattern. However, rather than using brighter Blaugrana shades, Nike has opted for a darker combination of Blue Void and Deep Garnet.

The two colours are the darkest shades previously featured in Barcelona's 2026/27 home shirt, which incorporated three different shades of blue and red.

Their use in the new design creates a more understated appearance while retaining the club's recognisable identity.

The latest replica images also showcase gold detailing around the sleeves and shoulder seams, adding contrast to the predominantly dark shirt.

Nike will reportedly use 'Mineral Yellow' for the Swoosh and selected design accents, providing a contrasting finish against the darker blue and maroon base. The shirt is also expected to feature a classic collar.

Barcelona's home kit for the 2027/28 season will feature a darker shade. (Source: Footy Headlines)

Other reported details include the Catalan Senyera flag on the back of the collar and the FC Barcelona Foundation logo towards the bottom of the back.

These elements maintain a connection with the club's identity beyond its traditional playing colours.

For what it is worth, the contrast between Barcelona's two leaked designs is particularly noticeable.

While the third kit embraces the visual influence of Correfoc through fire-inspired graphics, the home shirt prioritises the traditional vertical stripes that have long defined the club's appearance.

Debate it all you want, but Michigan vs Ohio State, in football, is the best rivalry in all of American sports.Alabama vs Auburn is as nasty as it gets, but that's a high-end, in-state war. Yankees vs Red Sox and Bears vs Packers – those get played several times a year. Duke vs North Carolina in basketball gets played at least twice. With Michigan and Ohio State, you have two behemoth universities from two different states, and it all comes down to this one game that, when it's at its biggest and best, stops the sports world cold.This isn't at its biggest and best this year, which means it's all about the rivalry. Trust me, you can be Michigan or Ohio State and win the national title, but if you don't beat the other, the season has a hole in it.As bad as the season has been for the Wolverines or Buckeyes, someone's year will be made.

Michigan finally got bowl-eligible with its thrilling win over UCLA last week.

Ohio State won 27-9 last year to break a run of four straight Michigan wins. The Buckeyes haven't beaten the Wolverines in Columbus since 2018.

The Michigan ground attack hasn't been too bad, and in this, it just has to keep the clock moving – having Bryce Underwood under center should help.Ohio State is 1-4 when allowing over 85 rushing yards. It won't have a problem if Michigan tries to keep running, but it does have to keep Underwood from finding a passing groove. The Buckeyes are now 0-4 against teams that connect on more than 60% of their passes. Underwood is hitting just 55% of his throws on the year.

Will Jeremiah Smith do enough to take home the Heisman? This is his one final chance to make his case, and Michigan will have him wrapped up tight. #2506. Maikel Garcia trade grades: Mariners land Gold Glove infielder; Royals get pitching help, but with huge risks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Kansas City Royals and Seattle Mariners have struck the offseason's first blockbuster trade. The Mariners have acquired third baseman Maikel Garcia in a six-player trade, the teams announced on Wednesday. The Royals receive righties Logan Evans and Bryce Miller and lefty Jose A. Ferrer in the deal.

Garcia, 26, battled hand and hamstring injuries in 2026, but still managed a 1.8 WAR season in 88 games thanks to league-average offense and spectacular third base defense. He is a year removed from a 5.6 WAR season and receiving MVP votes. Garcia is signed long-term as well. He's owed a very reasonable $52.5 million through 2030, with a club option for 2031.

The 28-year-old Miller headlines the return for Kansas City. An oblique strain delayed the start to his 2026 season, but once healthy, he threw 118 ⅔ innings with a 4.17 ERA and under-the-hood numbers that were hit (3.70 expected ERA) or miss (4.41 FIP). Miller threw 180 ⅓ innings with a 2.94 ERA in 2024, and will remain under team control through 2029.

Ferrer, 26, is a workhorse ground ball reliever with three years of control remaining. McArthur (fracture) and Evans (Tommy John) both missed 2026 with elbow surgery. McArthur pitched in four minor-league rehab games in September and should be ready for spring training. Evans has surgery in January and is expected back at midseason.

Here now are our grades for this three-for-three swap between 2027 American League postseason hopefuls.

The Mariners came into the offseason with an opening at third base, a glaring need to improve their defense, and more starters than rotation spots. That all came to a head in this trade. They used Miller, their least effective starter the last two seasons, and two spare parts to net a long-term solution at the hot corner in Garcia, who plays Gold Glove-caliber defense.

One player alone won't fix Seattle's defense, of course, but Garcia is a very big step toward improving a unit that ranked 26th in defensive runs saved and 30th (by a lot) in outs above average. As for the lineup, new manager Jason Kanzler can run out something like this most days:

Donovan was limited to 39 games by two groin strains and a concussion this past season. He's very versatile and needn't be locked into DH. The Mariners can play Donovan in the outfield to open up DH at-bats for slugger Lazaro Montes, who hit some titanic home runs during his MLB debut in 2026. They could also move Donovan around to give others DH days.

The lineup and the defense are improved, and the Mariners still have a formidable rotation that includes Kade Anderson, Logan Gilbert, Emerson Hancock, George Kirby, and Bryan Woo. Right-hander Ryan Sloan, arguably the top pitching prospect in baseball (it's either Sloan or Anderson), is knocking on the door and figures to debut at some point in 2027.

Seattle will miss Ferrer in their bullpen but also have close to an entire offseason (minus a lockout) to replace him. Assuming the Mariners won't break the bank for Adrian Morejon, the free agent market still offers solid second- and third-tier lefty reliever options in A.J. Minter, Sean Newcomb, JoJo Romero, Gregory Soto, and Alex Vesia. Ferrer is a quality reliever but not irreplaceable.

Before his elbow fracture, which ultimately required three surgeries, McArthur showed a very lively curveball and strong ground ball ability. He's a middle reliever more than a high-leverage option, but is not merely a throw-in. Langevin struck out 106 batters in 55 ⅓ Single-A relief innings thanks to his mid-90s fastball in 2026. He also walked 39 batters, however.

Garcia received MVP votes a year ago thanks to a .286/.351/.449 line with 16 home runs and 23 stolen bases. He also runs some of the game's best contact rates. That's his upside and maybe 2025 was a career year, but Garcia has a reasonably high floor thanks to his defense. Getting even league-average offense moving forward makes this a win for Seattle.

The free agent market is flush with No. 3-4 type starters and light on position players, specifically non-first base infielders. Couldn't the Royals keep Garcia and just sign a pitcher or two? There is something to be said for Miller's cost control as an arbitration-eligible player, of course, but he hasn't been healthy and effective at the same time since 2024. That's awfully risky.

Evans is a quality second piece as long as he bounces back well from Tommy John surgery. He made his MLB debut with the Mariners in 2025 and underwhelmed (4.32 ERA with iffy underlying numbers in 81 ⅓ innings), though he was regarded as a strong prospect before that, someone who should hold down a rotation spot for a long time.

Here's what FanGraphs wrote about Evans in June 2025, the last time he was prospect-eligible:

(His) sweeper is easily his best pitch, spins in at 2,800 rpm, and has hellacious lateral wipe. His reliance on it robs it of some bat-missing ability, and the last couple of years, the miss rate on Evans' slider has been pretty average because he's so often trying to throw it for strikes and hitters anticipate its arrival. But because Evans' fastball is fairly vulnerable, he's forced to lean on his breaking stuff ... Again, it's really only the sweeper that's plus, but Evans has a super deep repertoire, he throws a good rate of strikes and gets groundballs, and in 2024, he proved he could sustain this kind of stuff across more than 100 innings. Without a single pitch generating plus miss, he's probably not going to be a star, but he does enough to be a useful member of a big league rotation in a no. 4/5 capacity.

The Royals will have to wait for Evans to make an impact in their uniform because the timing of his Tommy John surgery means his rehab will extend into next spring and summer, but he is a quality second piece even if he is only a No. 4-5 starter. Cheap back-end starters are incredibly valuable and Evans should be that once his elbow is ready to go.

Ferrer could very well wind up closing games for the Royals this season and is a quality add to the bullpen. For Kansas City, the trade boils down to three things. One, can they keep Miller healthy and get him back to his 2024 form? He's the headliner in the trade and his success is imperative. Two, will Evans turn into a reliable rotation member once his elbow is sound?

And three, was Nick Loftin's 2026 for real? The Royals believe it was, hence trading Garcia. Loftin, 28, was a Gold Glove finalist this past season and he authored a .240/.322/.388 batting line with eight home runs in 118 games. If you're sold on Loftin as a league-average hitter and Gold Glove-caliber defender, well, that's what Garcia is, just without the name value.

The Royals badly needed rotation help -- there's no arguing that -- but they also ranked 22nd in runs this year and were middle of the pack defensively despite Loftin's (and Garcia's) glovework. There's a chance Kansas City made its position player core worse with only unspectacular pitching upgrades to show for it. I understand what they did. I just don't love it.

#2503. Re-grading the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade: Why the Heat and Bucks both look much worse now

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Giannis Antetokounmpo will face the Milwaukee Bucks for the first time as an opponent on Wednesday, but it's a game that feels as though it's a half-decade or more in the making. The Miami Heat were a rumored suitor for Antetokounmpo, who played his first 13 NBA seasons in Milwaukee, as far back as the buildup to his possible 2021 free agency, which the Bucks averted by trading for Jrue Holiday and ultimately winning a championship.

The Bucks kept kicking the can down the road. They secured another extension with Antetokounmpo in 2023 by trading for Damian Lillard. They stuck their fingers in their ears and pretended everything was fine when Lillard tore his Achilles in 2025, in the process bypassing the chance to trade Antetokounmpo with multiple years left on his contract when they could have maximized his trade value. In the end, though, Heat president Pat Riley did what he has done so many times before: he got his man.

Now, Antetokounmpo plays for the Heat while the Bucks are in no man's land. We have around four weeks of data on how these teams are going to look after one of the bigger blockbusters in recent NBA history, so with their first head-to-head bout at hand, let's regrade the trade based on everything we now know.

Let's start with the obvious positive: despite age- and injury-related fears, Antetokounmpo is still mostly himself. He is, by both the counting stats and the all-in-ones, playing either at the level of his Milwaukee peak or somewhere relatively close. He has at the very least been a top 10 player in the NBA this season, and you could argue him into the top five. Miami paid an All-NBA price and has gotten an All-NBA player.

There are slight signs of slipping in his age-32 season that merit some examination, though they don't come close to triggering any real alarms. His free-throw rate is lower than it's been since 2018, for instance, but it's still near the top of the league. He's scoring 1.38 points per possession when shooting at the rim -- a very good figure that rates him in the 82nd percentile league-wide, per Synergy Sports. We just judge Antetokounmpo on a curve because he was in the 95th percentile last season and generally hovered around the mid-90s when he was winning MVPs and his 2021 championship.

This is, again, not a significant concern. He's still great, and he's supplementing his rim finishing with significant improvement from mid-range. After shooting below 39% from mid-range over the past five seasons combined, he's above 51% so far this season. We can say pretty safely at this point that the 3-point shot is never coming for Antetokounmpo, so this shot will be his pathway to both aging gracefully and combating the walls he'll see at the rim in the playoffs. If this is sustainable, it extends his prime another year or two and makes him close to unguardable while he remains near his physical peak. Thus far, last year's calf injuries have not recurred.

He's slipped defensively. That's almost undeniable. He contested around nine shots per game when he won Defensive Player of the Year in 2020. He's down to around six this season, and opponents are shooting 6% worse within six feet of the basket against Antetokounmpo than they are otherwise, per NBA.com tracking data. That figure was 20.4% in 2020. The all-in-ones share this basic opinion: still good, no longer great. The tape shows an older player who paces himself defensively. He can still summon greatness for stretches, but he's not in the All-Defense mix seriously anymore.

That brings us to the bigger picture. When you trade as much as Miami did, the question is never just whether the player is good enough to justify the cost, but whether the team is. Heat fans would point to the team's ongoing 8-2 stretch following its 0-4 start to suggest that it was. Count me as a remaining skeptic.

Most of those victories came against either the bottom of the league -- the Kings, the Jazz, they needed overtime to beat the Clippers! -- or injured opponents. No Tyrese Haliburton in the Pacers win. No Jalen Duren against the Pistons. No Evan Mobley against the Cavaliers. No Amen Thompson against the Rockets, playing the second night of a back-to-back. They've faced only two true heavy hitters at full strength, the Lakers and Timberwolves, and they stood no chance against either.

The theory of this team relies on a top-five defense. The offense is simply too reliant on shot creation out of its bigs -- Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo -- to be the leading unit for a champion. The early defensive returns have thus far been discouraging, though in fairness, no team has been unluckier on wide-open opponents' 3s. Even during the 8-2 stretch, they're allowing 48.4 points in the paint per game, a well-below-average figure. Their transition defense is nothing special and they're so-so rebounders. They've hung their hat on turnover-generation, but they're by no means elite on that front. The raw numbers are bad. The truth is closer to fine when you factor in luck. They haven't been great, which is what they need to be.

Part of the problem is that they need to play defensively deficient players -- most notably Klay Thompson and, if he eventually re-earns his rotation spot, Tim Hardaway Jr. -- in order to survive offensively. You can get away with that if everyone else is great. Antetokounmpo has taken a step back. Andrew Wiggins has been a mess. Erik Spoelstra is a defensive miracle worker, but the players here just haven't lived up to expectations. Davion Mitchell has become so important offensively that even he's slipped a bit on that end.

Mitchell's playmaking has been a godsend, and a pretty surprising one in context. The Heat tried and failed to get the Bucks to take Mitchell instead of Kasparas Jakučionis in the trade. There's no telling how bad things would be without Mitchell at this stage, but we're still talking about a pretty limited scorer who nearly doubled his 3-point volume and free throw attempt rate in a single season. Miami probably can't expect him to carry this sort of burden forever. Pelle Larsson is more of a connector than a creator in his own right. Down the line, another guard who can create off of the dribble is probably needed here, especially without a strong Antetokounmpo-Adebayo two-man game forming thus far.

The paths to improvement here are narrow here. The Heat are pressed up against a first-apron hard cap, and they'd need Charlotte's cooperation to amend the protection on their 2027 selection if they wanted to trade even a single first-round pick at this deadline. It's going to take a little while to meaningfully upgrade the supporting talent here, and the rest of the Heat offseason reflected that.

They could have perhaps generated the cap flexibility to retain Norman Powell. They elected instead to let him walk, and when they extended Wiggins, they chose to front-load the deal by using his player option rather than spreading the money out to create more immediate hard cap room. Rather than signing a mid-level free agent to a multi-year deal, they added the older Hardaway on just a one-year contract, presumably to maintain optionality going into next summer.

If Antetokounmpo were 28, this patience might make sense. He turns 32 in less than a month. The time to go all-in around him is now. It's an ironic middle ground that the Heat have put themselves in. Miami could justify the cost it paid for Antetokounmpo only through immediate contention, yet they're slow-playing the roster build in what you would expect, just based on the standard aging curve, to be the best individual season left in his career. It really doesn't make sense to do this halfway.

We're talking about the Heat here. They've made the Finals with less talent than they have now, and they are organizationally opposed to intentional rebuilds. There was never a conversation here about, say, trading Adebayo and starting over as opposed to pushing chips in for someone like Antetokounmpo. But if a few years pass and the Heat don't at least make the conference finals with this core, it's going to be worth wondering if that's the path they should have taken. The early returns here are mixed. The Heat bet their future on a single player. He may be good enough to warrant that investment, but the jury's still out on whether their team actually is.

The Bucks dug themselves an enormous hole by refusing to trade Antetokounmpo when the whole world knew they should have. It was over the moment Lillard tore his Achilles. At that point, Antetokounmpo had two years left on his contract, so hypothetical rental trades would have been feasible. He was younger and he hadn't yet lost a year to calf injuries, so his value was higher. Asset-rich teams like the Spurs and Rockets might have been interested. Had the Bucks moved Antetokounmpo in 2025, they would have gotten substantially more than they wound up getting. Instead, they made the disastrous decision not only to keep him but also to waive and stretch Lillard to sign Myles Turner. Yikes.

When the Bucks finally realized they'd reached the point of no return, Antetokounmpo, as an expiring contract, had complete control of the situation. At least four teams with strong offers were turned away because Antetokounmpo simply wasn't interested in extending with them, according to ESPN. He only wanted the Heat or Celtics. Given those circumstances, the Bucks still managed the negotiations as well as they reasonably could have. They used the Celtics as an effective scare tactic to compel Miami to give up pretty much all of its available draft capital, plus Jakučionis instead of Mitchell.

You can win a negotiation and still lose a trade, though, when most of the things the other team had to give in a trade just weren't that valuable. The big swing piece here was Kel'El Ware, an extremely high-risk, high-reward young big man with star-level raw talent and a pretty iffy reputation when it comes to his motor and commitment. The Bucks, thus far, have gotten the worst version of him. He's playing less in his third season with the Bucks than he did in two years with the Heat despite being on the worst roster of his career. He's missing shots everywhere, his defense has been miserable, and if he's ever going to reach that sky-high ceiling, it's probably going to have to come on his third team.

That, in a nutshell, is the problem here. The Bucks traded the greatest player in franchise history, one of the 25 or so best players the league has ever seen, and got no one who could credibly be considered a cornerstone moving forward. Ware looks like a swing and a miss. It's too early to say much on Nate Ament, but he's a No. 13 overall draft pick, so odds are, he's going to be fine and not much better. Tyler Herro and Jaime Jaquez Jr. are both about what they expected, but both will need to be paid next summer. Herro's presence exacerbates a preexisting glut of guards. His presence has forced last year's breakout guard, Ryan Rollins, to the bench. Maybe that makes him a bit cheaper as a free agent next summer. It also probably sours him on a future in Milwaukee.

Speaking of the guard glut, the Gary Trent Jr. investigation looms large over this trade. The NBA set a notable precedent in the Kawhi Leonard case that it is willing to strip teams of draft picks acquired through trade. This is notable because the Bucks have so little control over their own first-round picks moving forward. The picks they got from the Heat in 2031 and 2033, at least for now, are the crown jewels of this trade. Both of them are theoretically vulnerable if the NBA finds that the Bucks circumvented the salary cap.

It's even worth wondering if the Bucks should or could have used the Antetokounmpo situation as an escape hatch on any preexisting agreements with Trent, if one actually existed. If the Bucks felt an obligation to pay Trent more than the market suggested he was worth, and if they knew they had so many guards that he was unlikely to factor into their rotation (he played less than 40 total minutes before bizarrely leading the Bucks in playing time in Sunday's loss to the Hawks despite coming off the bench), then why not use the leverage Antetokounmpo's availability granted them to foist Trent on Miami through a sign-and-trade? Of course, if the Bucks had the foresight to do this, they probably wouldn't be in this situation in the first place. For now, the investigation is ongoing and we know little beyond the sheer ridiculousness of the contract itself.

The Bucks are 1-13 as of this writing. That, roughly, was to be expected. This was a bad team with Antetokounmpo, so inevitably, removing an MVP candidate was going to make it far worse. But to leave a trade involving a player of that caliber without a single blue-chip player or draft pick is frankly embarrassing.

The Bucks bungled this Antetokounmpo saga for a year, and even if they managed its end stages properly, they'd dug themselves so deep a hole that there was just no obvious way out of it. Now, it seems they may well have made the situation worse with Trent after the fact. This was an organization-wide debacle.

#2502. MLB rumors: Tarik Skubal hosts more meetings, Red Sox add backup catcher, plus Padres, Phillies, Rays, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The hot stove is starting to heat up. On Tuesday, David Bednar and Ryan Jeffers accepted the $23.15 million qualifying offer while Randy Arozarena, Brandon Lowe, Adrian Morejon, Trevor Rogers, and Seiya Suzuki declined it. Those five are now attached to draft pick compensation. Also, the White Sox landed righty Dustin May on a three-year contract.

We're still waiting on the offseason's first real blockbuster but things are beginning to pick up. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Wednesday's hot stove happenings.

The Red Sox have acquired catcher Nick Fortes from the AL East rival Rays for 17-year-old minor-league righty Angel Roa, the team announced on Wednesday. Fortes will take over as Adley Rutschman's backup catcher. He is projected to make $3.4 million or so through arbitration in 2027, which is a pricey sum for a backup catcher, particularly for a small payroll team like the Rays. Connor Wong has been designated for assignment by the Red Sox in a corresponding move.

Fortes, 30, had a career-best season at the plate in 2026, though his defensive numbers took a big dip. The Rays acquired Liam Hicks at the trade deadline and he is their clear-cut starting catcher. Kenny Piper, who made his MLB debut in August, could step in as the backup until top prospect Caden Bodine is ready, which could be as soon as next summer.

The Blue Jays and Dodgers had in-person meetings with top-ranked free agent Tarik Skubal on Tuesday, reports ESPN. He will meet with the Padres later this week and already met with the Mets on Monday. Rival executives expect it to come down to Blue Jays and Mets, per ESPN. Toronto has a history of pursuing top free agents but missing out (Shohei Ohtani, Kyle Tucker, etc.).

Skubal is expected to sign before the lockout and is therefore working on a tight schedule, much tighter than usual for top Scott Boras clients. The Dodgers are said to have interest in a short-term contract with a large annual salary, something that is unlikely to appeal to Skubal. He's poised to land a record contract for a pitcher, perhaps even more than $400 million.

Star shortstop Corey Seager has expressed an openness to a trade to only a "handful of teams," reports ESPN. Seager has a full no-trade clause and can pick his destination, and was reportedly quite picky as a free agent five years ago. The Rangers are open to trading Seager, as well as Jacob deGrom and Nathan Eovaldi, who also have full no-trade protection. deGrom already reportedly invoked his no-trade clause at last season's deadline to spike a deal to the Braves.

Seager, 33 in April, had surgery to remove a bone spur from his elbow last month, and was limited to 102 games by injuries in 2026. When healthy, he has typically beibeeng very good, but the injuries and surgeries are mounting. Seager is owed $31 million annually through 2031. Texas would likely have to eat some money to facilitate a trade.

On Tuesday, the Padres hosted free agent outfielder Seiya Suzuki for a recruiting visit, according to ESPN. San Diego aggressively pursued Suzuki when he initially came over from Japan five years ago, but he opted to sign with the Cubs instead. We ranked Suzuki as the seventh-best free agent available this offseason, and the third-best free agent position player.

San Diego needs rotation help more than anything this offseason, though they could use another middle-of-the-lineup bat as well. They could sign Suzuki, plant him in right field, and move Fernando Tatis Jr. back to the infield, where he played 53 games at second base this past season. It was Tatis' first action on the infield since he was the team's starting shortstop in 2021.

After signing Jake Bauers, president of baseball operations Craig Breslow said it is "hard to envision that there's something significant on the horizon" for the Red Sox, according to the Boston Globe. That doesn't mean the Red Sox won't do something significant later in the offseason, perhaps after the lockout, but, right now, there is nothing major in the works.

Breslow's next order of business is unclogging his outfield/DH logjam, which could involve trading or even non-tendering Jarren Duran. The Red Sox also have four pitchers for the No. 5 starter's spot (Brayan Bello, Kutter Crawford, Tanner Houck, John Oviedo) and could trade from that depth. Otherwise, Boston has no glaring roster issues remaining this offseason.

Free agent slugger Randy Arozarena is seeking well over $100 million and could end up waiting until after the lockout to sign, according to ESPN. For now, teams are balking at that asking price, but that isn't unusual this early in the offseason. The Orioles and Yankees are among the clubs reported to have interest in Arozarena, our ninth-ranked free agent.

Although Arozarena had the better 2026 season, Suzuki is considered the more desirable free agent because he's a much better defender. They're roughly the same age and are comparable hitters, but Arozarena is a borderline DH at this point. Right-handed power is in shockingly short supply, though. He (and Suzuki) would improve almost any lineup. As noted above, both players declined the qualifying offer from their respective teams, which means they are tagged with draft pick compensation.

The Phillies are receiving trade calls about righty reliever Orion Kerkering, reports The Athletic. Kerkering struggled badly in the second half, allowing 25 runs and 43 baserunners in his final 19 ⅓ MLB innings of the season. The Phillies optioned him to Triple-A a week before the end of the regular season and did not carry him on their Wild Card Series roster.

Still only 25, Kerkering has a history of missing bats at a high level and experience in late-inning situations. He will remain under team control through 2029. The Phillies certainly don't have to trade him. They could keep him and even send him to Triple-A next season. It never hurts to listen, however, and other teams presumably see Kerkering as a buy-low candidate.

Veteran righty Frankie Montas hit 98 mph and wowed scouts during a workout in Arizona this week, reports The Athletic. Multiple general managers were in attendance, and it's possible Montas will land a guaranteed major-league contract. He is rehabbing from Tommy John surgery and has not pitched in an MLB game since August 2025.

Pitching is always in demand, especially cheap pitching with upside behind league-average innings. Montas, 34 in March, has not been healthy and effective at the same time since 2022, though he looked good during his showcase and he has a reputation for being an excellent teammate who mentors young pitchers. That will only help his case.

If entering the protocol does force Herbert to miss time, the Chargers would turn to DJ Uiagalelei. He has played in one NFL game, in mop-up duty against the Texans in Week 9. He went 2-for-7 for 24 yards and a touchdown. Los Angeles also has Jake Browning on the practice squad.
